eintraege.titel: Buying a house with a mortgage in Germany
tags: am i allowed to finance a house
eintraege.text: The starting point is clear: the Quran permits trade and forbids interest, and a classic bank loan with interest falls under that. For buying a house in the West, scholars have therefore first looked for interest-free ways: Islamic financing models such as Murabaha (the bank buys and resells at an agreed mark-up) or Musharaka (joint ownership with a step-by-step buy-out); such offers now exist in German-speaking countries too. In addition, cooperative models, saving up until you can pay cash, and an interest-free purchase through the family are widespread. Some scholars have considered exceptions for minority situations, for an owner-occupied home when no interest-free alternative is within reach; others reject this. This difference of opinion is well known and serious — whoever has to decide should put their concrete situation to a scholar instead of relying on a blanket answer.

Holding shares in a company is permitted in principle, because it is a stake in a real business, not in interest. The examination starts with the business model: companies whose core business is alcohol, gambling, interest-based lending, pornography or the arms trade are ruled out. Because hardly any corporation is completely free of interest income, scholarly bodies have developed threshold values for how much interest share and debt is bearable, and they require that the impure part of the earnings be given away. In practice this is reflected by Sharia-compliant indices and matching ETFs. Speculation with a high degree of uncertainty, short selling and leveraged trading, by contrast, are rejected by the majority because they come close to gambling. On cryptocurrencies opinions differ: some scholars see them as a tradable good, others reject them because of a lack of intrinsic value and heavy volatility. Investment assets are also subject to Zakat every year.

Conventional insurance is disputed among scholars, because it can contain elements of uncertainty, interest and gambling: you pay a fixed sum for an uncertain compensation. There is broad agreement about the policies that are legally required in Germany — motor liability insurance and health insurance: what the state demands as compulsory counts as a necessity that you comply with; here the principle applies that the religion imposes no hardship. With voluntary contracts, especially with endowment life insurance that earns interest, many scholars advise restraint and point to Takaful, the cooperative model of mutual protection, as well as to savings reserves and family solidarity. Pure risk cover without a savings component is judged considerably more leniently by some scholars. If you want a particular policy examined, present the concrete contract — the assessment depends on its terms.

According to the Quran, what is forbidden is carrion, blood, pork and anything slaughtered over which a name other than Allah's was invoked; everything else is permitted in principle. In practice it therefore comes down to the origin of the ingredients. Gelatine usually comes from pigs or cattle — beef gelatine is regarded as unproblematic when the slaughter was done properly, pork gelatine is not; some scholars view it as a new substance because of the heavy transformation, but the majority does not follow this. E numbers on their own say nothing: a few, such as E120 (carmine, from scale insects) or E441 (gelatine), point to animal origin, most are plant-based or synthetic. Flavourings can contain alcohol as a carrier substance; if it is present only in tiny, non-intoxicating residual amounts and is technically unavoidable, many scholars consider it unproblematic, others advise against it. Salati has the Halal scanner for this: scan the barcode, read the ingredient list in plain words. When in doubt, asking the manufacturer helps.

eintraege.titel: Medicines and vaccines with critical ingredients
tags: am i allowed to take this
eintraege.text: Among the forbidden foods the Quran explicitly names the case of compulsion: whoever is forced, without desiring it and without exceeding the limit, bears no sin. On this basis scholars largely agree that necessary medicines may be taken even when they contain alcohol as a solvent or gelatine in the capsule shell, as long as no equivalent alternative is available. The same applies to vaccines: the major contemporary scholarly bodies have ranked the protection of life and health as taking precedence. It still makes sense to ask at the pharmacy for an alcohol-free or plant-based version — often there is one. The assessment changes when a substance does not serve healing but pleasure. For a concrete treatment decision, the doctor and, in case of doubt, a scholar should be asked together.

eintraege.titel: Working where alcohol or pork is sold
tags: am i allowed to work there
eintraege.text: The Quran calls intoxicating drink a work of Satan and urges people to help one another to goodness and God-consciousness, not to sin and transgression; it is also reported that with wine the one who pours it and the one who transports it were cursed as well. Scholars therefore judge activities with differing strictness, depending on how close they stand to the forbidden thing: pouring, delivering or selling alcohol is predominantly rejected; at a supermarket checkout, where among many goods alcohol or pork occasionally passes over the belt, many scholars by contrast see no direct participation — especially when no other workplace is within reach and a family has to be provided for. The recommendation is to look for a solution together with the employer, for example by swapping areas of responsibility, and to aim for an alternative in the medium term. For your own situation, speaking directly with a scholar is the right way.

eintraege.titel: Friday prayer and Eid in everyday working life in Germany
eintraege.text: The Quran calls on believers to let trading rest when the call to the Friday prayer comes and to go back to work afterwards — prayer and profession therefore do not exclude each other. In Germany there is no legal entitlement to a prayer break, but there is the possibility of agreeing one in the employment contract, through the break arrangement or with your supervisor; in practice Jumu'ah can usually be solved with a shifted lunch break and compensatory time. For the two Eid days you take holiday; many companies grant it without trouble if it is announced early, since the dates are fixed a year in advance. For pupils, the school laws of the federal states provide for leave of absence on religious grounds, which is applied for informally. Whoever cannot reach the Friday prayer because of work prays Dhuhr instead — no sin arises from that. Salati can remind you of Jumu'ah and the Eid dates in good time.

eintraege.titel: The Salam — how Muslims greet one another
eintraege.text: The Islamic greeting is “As-salamu alaikum wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh” — “Peace be upon you, and Allah's mercy and His blessing”. Whoever is greeted answers “Wa alaikumu s-salam wa rahmatullahi wa barakatuh” — “And upon you be peace, and Allah's mercy and His blessing”. A shorter form works too: “As-salamu alaikum”, with the reply “Wa alaikumu s-salam”. The Quran requires a greeting to be returned with a better one, or at least to be given back as an equal. You also greet when entering houses — other people's houses only after making yourself noticed. The Salam is not a mere “hello”: you wish the other person peace and mercy, and that is exactly what creates closeness, even between strangers.

eintraege.titel: Dua — how to ask and when it is answered especially
tags: how do i pray for something
eintraege.text: Dua means addressing Allah directly — in any language, in any place, without an intermediary. Allah says: “Call upon Me, I will respond to you” and “I am near; I answer the call of the caller when he calls upon Me”. It is good to begin with praise of Allah and the blessing upon the Prophet ﷺ, to call upon Him by His most beautiful names, and to ask humbly, quietly and without haste. Regarded as especially open are the last third of the night, the time between the Adhan and the Iqama, the moment of prostration, the Friday hour, the instant of breaking the fast, and travel. Lawful income matters too: the Prophet ﷺ described a traveller who stretches his hands to the sky while his food, drink and clothing are unlawful — “how then should he be answered?” And whoever does not receive at once what he asks for has not been turned away; scholars recall that Allah either gives, or wards off an evil, or stores it up for the Hereafter.

tags: what do you say before eating
eintraege.text: Before eating you say “Bismillah” — “In the name of Allah”. Whoever has forgotten it and only thinks of it halfway through says “Bismillahi fi awwalihi wa akhirih” — “In the name of Allah, at its beginning and at its end”. After eating it is reported: “Alhamdu lillahil-ladhi at'amani hadha wa razaqanihi min ghairi haulin minni wa la quwwa” — “All praise belongs to Allah, who let me eat this and provided it for me, without any power or strength of my own”. For the host you pray “Allahumma barik lahum fima razaqtahum, waghfir lahum warhamhum” — “O Allah, bless them in what You have provided for them, forgive them and have mercy on them”. The Quran links eating and gratitude directly: “Eat of the good things with which We have provided you, and be grateful to Allah.”

eintraege.titel: Supplication when leaving and entering the house
tags: what do you say when leaving the house
eintraege.text: When leaving the house you say “Bismillahi tawakkaltu ala Allah, wa la haula wa la quwwata illa billah” — “In the name of Allah, I put my trust in Allah, and there is no power and no strength except with Allah”. For coming home it is reported: “Bismillahi walajna, wa bismillahi kharajna, wa ala Allahi Rabbina tawakkalna” — “In the name of Allah we enter, in the name of Allah we go out, and upon Allah, our Lord, we rely”. Both are short sentences that set the day in the right frame: I set out with Allah's name, not with my own strength. The Quran says about this: “Whoever puts his trust in Allah, He is sufficient for him.” And whoever arrives at home can speak the greeting — the Salam belongs to your own family as well.

eintraege.titel: Supplication for going to sleep and for waking up
tags: what do you say before falling asleep
eintraege.text: Before falling asleep you say “Bismika Allahumma amutu wa ahya” — “In Your name, O Allah, I die and I live”. Whoever lies down can add: “Bismika Rabbi wada'tu janbi wa bika arfa'uh, fa-in amsakta nafsi farhamha, wa in arsaltaha fahfazha bima tahfazu bihi ibadakas-salihin” — “In Your name, my Lord, I lay down my side, and through You I raise it again. If You hold back my soul, then have mercy on it, and if You send it back, then guard it as You guard Your righteous servants”. On waking up you say “Alhamdu lillahil-ladhi ahyana ba'da ma amatana wa ilaihin-nushur” — “All praise belongs to Allah, who gave us life after He had caused us to die (sleep), and to Him is the resurrection”. The Quran calls sleep a sign of Allah, a rest for the body and at the same time a small form of dying: Allah takes the souls, holds one back and releases the other for an appointed term.

tags: what do you say when driving
eintraege.text: When setting off you say the travel supplication that the Quran itself provides: “Subhanal-ladhi sakhkhara lana hadha wa ma kunna lahu muqrinin, wa inna ila Rabbina lamunqalibun” — “Glory be to Him who has made this subservient to us, while we ourselves could not have managed it. And truly, to our Lord we shall return”. For the return home it is reported: “Ayibuna ta'ibuna abiduna li-Rabbina hamidun” — “We return, we repent, we worship and we praise our Lord”. Whoever sees someone off says “Astaudi'ullaha dinaka wa amanataka wa khawatima amalik” — “I entrust to Allah your religion, what is placed in your trust, and the outcome of your deeds”. Travel counts as a time in which supplications are accepted especially — and the Quran reminds us that the best provision for the journey is God-consciousness.

tags: what do you say when someone sneezes
eintraege.text: Whoever sneezes says “Alhamdulillah” — “All praise belongs to Allah”. Whoever hears it answers “Yarhamukallah” — “May Allah have mercy on you”. That is more than politeness: a tiny everyday moment turns into gratitude and into a supplication for one another. The Prophet ﷺ said that “Alhamdulillah” fills the scale — a word that is light to pronounce and heavy in weight. Whoever does not know the reply can say something friendly in their own language; the formula shuts nobody out.

eintraege.titel: Supplication when entering and leaving the mosque
tags: what do you say in the mosque
eintraege.text: When entering the mosque you say “Allahumma iftah li abwaba rahmatik” — “O Allah, open for me the gates of Your mercy”. When going out you say “Allahumma inni as'aluka min fadlik” — “O Allah, I ask You for Your bounty”. Common practice is to step in with the right foot and to pray two rak'ah before sitting down (Tahiyyat al-Masjid), unless the congregational prayer is just beginning. Quiet applies in the mosque: no loud worldly conversation, no pushing, phone on silent. The Quran says: “The places of worship belong to Allah, so call upon no one besides Allah” — the mosque is a place where everything is aligned towards Him. And to visit it is itself a sign of faith: “Only he maintains Allah's places of worship who believes in Allah and the Last Day.”

eintraege.titel: Supplication before and after the toilet
tags: what do you say before the toilet
eintraege.text: Before entering the toilet you say “Allahumma inni a'udhu bika minal-khubuthi wal-khaba'ith” — “O Allah, I seek refuge with You from the male and female devils”. When going out you say “Ghufranak” — “(I ask for) Your forgiveness”. Both are very short sentences that are easy to learn; you speak them quietly or in your heart before you step in. Common practice is to go in with the left foot and out with the right, and not to carry the name of Allah into that room. The background is the high importance of purity: “Purity is half of faith”, said the Prophet ﷺ, and the Quran says that Allah loves those who keep themselves pure.

eintraege.titel: Supplication in worry, fear and pressure
tags: what to do when i feel bad
eintraege.text: For worry and grief it is reported: “Allahumma inni a'udhu bika minal-hammi wal-hazan, wal-'ajzi wal-kasal, wal-bukhli wal-jubn, wa dala'id-dayni wa ghalabatir-rijal” — “O Allah, I seek refuge with You from worry and grief, from incapacity and laziness, from miserliness and cowardice, from the burden of debt and from being overpowered by people”. Very short and very strong is the supplication of Yunus: “La ilaha illa anta subhanaka inni kuntu minaz-zalimin” — “There is no god but You. Glory be to You! I was truly among the wrongdoers”. When fear of people or of circumstances weighs on you, you say “Hasbunallahu wa ni'mal-wakil” — “Allah is sufficient for us, and He is the best disposer of affairs”. The Quran promises: “In the remembrance of Allah hearts find rest” and “with hardship comes ease”. Supplication and medical or psychological help do not exclude each other — you may and should use both.

eintraege.titel: Supplication in illness and when visiting the sick
tags: what do you say to someone who is ill
eintraege.text: For someone who is ill you pray: “Allahumma Rabban-nas, adhhibil-ba's, ishfi wa antash-Shafi, la shifa'a illa shifa'uk, shifa'an la yughadiru saqama” — “O Allah, Lord of humankind, take the affliction away. Heal, for You are the Healer. There is no healing except Your healing — a healing that leaves no illness behind”. When visiting the sick it is reported to say seven times: “As'alullahal-'Azima Rabbal-'arshil-'azimi an yashfiyak” — “I ask Allah the Mighty, the Lord of the mighty Throne, to heal you”. In case of pain you put your hand on the spot, say “Bismillah” three times and then seven times “A'udhu billahi wa qudratihi min sharri ma ajidu wa uhadhir” — “I seek refuge with Allah and His power from the evil of what I feel and fear”. The Quran has Ibrahim say: “and who, when I am ill, heals me” — healing comes from Allah, medical treatment is the way to it, no contradiction. Illness is at the same time a test, and glad tidings are for those who endure: they are the ones who say “We belong to Allah, and to Him we return”.

tags: what do you say when someone passes away
eintraege.text: When news of a death arrives, you say “Inna lillahi wa inna ilaihi raji'un” — “Truly, we belong to Allah, and truly, to Him we return”. In the funeral prayer it is reported: “Allahumma-ghfir lihayyina wa mayyitina, wa shahidina wa gha'ibina, wa saghirina wa kabirina, wa dhakarina wa unthana” — “O Allah, forgive our living and our dead, those of us present and those absent, our young and our old, our men and our women”. When visiting graves you greet: “As-salamu alaikum ahlad-diyari minal-mu'minina wal-muslimin” — “Peace be upon you, dwellers of these abodes, believers and Muslims”. For parents and for brothers and sisters in faith, the Quran names ready-made words: “Our Lord, forgive us and our brothers who preceded us in faith” and “Our Lord, forgive me and my parents”. The sincere supplication is the best gift you can still give to someone who has passed away.

The Quran calls on believers to remember Allah much and to glorify Him “morning and evening” — out of this a firm habit has grown: the adhkar in the morning (after Fajr) and in the evening (after Asr or Maghrib). You begin, for example, with “Asbahna wa asbahal-mulku lillah, walhamdu lillah” — “We have entered the morning, and with us the dominion of Allah, and all praise belongs to Allah”; in the evening it is “Amsaina wa amsal-mulku lillah, walhamdu lillah”. Among others there belongs “Raditu billahi Rabban, wa bil-islami dinan, wa bi-Muhammadin sallallahu alaihi wa sallama nabiyya” — “I am content with Allah as Lord, with Islam as religion and with Muhammad ﷺ as Prophet” — and the sentence of protection “Bismillahil-ladhi la yadurru ma'a ismihi shai'un fil-ardi wa la fis-sama'i wa huwas-Sami'ul-'Alim”, spoken three times. More important than the quantity is constancy: better three formulas every day than twenty once a week.

eintraege.titel: Dhikr after the obligatory prayer (33/33/34 and Ayat al-Kursi)
tags: what do you do after prayer
eintraege.text: After every obligatory prayer there is a small fixed programme. You say three times “Astaghfirullah” — “I ask Allah for forgiveness” — and then “Allahumma antas-salamu wa minkas-salam, tabarakta ya dhal-jalali wal-ikram” — “O Allah, You are Peace and from You comes peace. Blessed are You, O Owner of Majesty and Honour”. After that follow 33 times “Subhanallah” (Glory be to Allah), 33 times “Alhamdulillah” (All praise belongs to Allah) and 34 times “Allahu akbar” (Allah is greater); in another version 33 times Allahu akbar and, as the hundredth, the Tahlil: “La ilaha illallahu wahdahu la sharika lah, lahul-mulku wa lahul-hamd, wa huwa ala kulli shai'in qadir”. Afterwards you recite Ayat al-Kursi (Quran 2:255). The Quran itself links prayer and remembrance: “When you have completed the prayer, remember Allah standing, sitting and on your sides.”

eintraege.titel: Salawat — the blessing upon the Prophet ﷺ
tags: what does the symbol after muhammad mean
eintraege.text: When the name of the Prophet Muhammad is mentioned, you speak the blessing: “Sallallahu alaihi wa sallam” — “May Allah's blessing and peace be upon him”. The small symbol ﷺ in Islamic texts and in this app stands for it as well. The Quran gives the reason: “Allah and His angels send blessings upon the Prophet. O you who believe, send blessings upon him and greet him with a proper greeting.” In the prayer, the detailed form is spoken after the Tashahhud, the so-called Ibrahimic formula. Salawat are an easy remembrance, possible at any time — many Muslims speak them especially often on Friday, for the one who was sent as a mercy to the worlds.

eintraege.titel: Istighfar and tawbah — asking for forgiveness and turning back
eintraege.text: Istighfar means asking Allah for forgiveness — at its shortest with “Astaghfirullaha wa atubu ilaih” — “I ask Allah for forgiveness and turn to Him in repentance”. The most comprehensive formula is called Sayyid al-Istighfar and begins: “Allahumma anta Rabbi la ilaha illa ant, khalaqtani wa ana abduk…” — “O Allah, You are my Lord, there is no god but You. You created me, and I am Your servant…”, and it ends with “so forgive me, for no one forgives sins except You”. Tawbah is more than the words: stopping, regretting sincerely, resolving firmly not to repeat it — and where people have been wronged, giving their right back to them or asking them for pardon. The Quran leaves no doubt: “Do not lose hope in Allah's mercy. Truly, Allah forgives all sins.” In a Hadith Qudsi it says: “As long as you call upon Me and hope in Me, I forgive you whatever came from you.”
belege: an-Nawawī Nr. 42 — Sunan at-Tirmidhi (hasan, Hadith Qudsi)

eintraege.text: “Bismillahir-Rahmanir-Rahim” means “In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful”. The Fatihah begins with this sentence, and it stands at the start of almost every Surah of the Quran. In everyday life the short form “Bismillah” — “In the name of Allah” — is often enough: before eating, before wudu, when setting off, before work, when entering the house. The formula is not a magic spell but an orientation: I do not begin this matter out of my own strength and not for myself alone, but with the name of the One who has made mercy His own attribute. The Quran also shows it as a formula of the prophets — Nuh spoke it when boarding the ship, and Sulaiman's letter began with it.

eintraege.titel: In sha Allah, ma sha Allah, alhamdulillah — the everyday formulas
eintraege.text: “In sha Allah” means “if Allah wills” and belongs with every plan for the future; the Quran says explicitly that you should never claim about a matter “I will do this tomorrow” without adding “if Allah wills”. “Ma sha Allah” means “what Allah has willed” and is said when you see something beautiful — in the Quran linked with “there is no power except through Allah”, so that admiration does not tip over into envy. “Alhamdulillah” means “all praise belongs to Allah” and is the answer to good things as well as to everyday ones; Allah promises: “If you are grateful, I will surely give you more.” Added to these are “Subhanallah” (Glory be to Allah) when you are amazed, “Astaghfirullah” (I ask Allah for forgiveness) after a mistake, and “Jazakallahu khairan” — “May Allah reward you with good” — as thanks to a person. These formulas are not empty phrases: they anchor the whole day in the remembrance of Allah.

The Quran places kindness to parents directly after the acknowledgement of Allah: “And your Lord has decreed that you worship none but Him, and that you be kind to your parents.” When they grow old, you may not even say an annoyed “ugh!”, but should speak respectfully and lower “the wing of humility”. For this the Quran gives a ready-made supplication: “Rabbi irhamhuma kama rabbayani saghira” — “My Lord, have mercy on them both, as they raised me when I was small”. The mother is singled out in particular, who carried and gave birth in weakness. If parents demand something that contradicts Allah, they are not obeyed in that — but dealing with them still stays friendly and decent; in difficult family situations it is wise to ask a knowledgeable person or a scholar for advice. Even after their death the way remains open: supplication, Sadaqah and keeping up the ties they had.

In one line with parents and relatives the Quran explicitly names “the neighbour who is a relative, the neighbour who is a stranger, the companion at your side” — neighbourliness is therefore a right of its own, independent of religion or kinship. The Prophet ﷺ said: “Whoever believes in Allah and the Last Day, let him honour his neighbour”, and in the same breath: “let him speak good or stay silent” and “let him honour his guest”. In practice that means: no noise and no rubbish at the expense of others, greeting people, helping in illness or when moving house, sharing something of your food, overlooking faults. Whoever takes a hardship off another, Allah takes a hardship off him on the Day of Judgement — that holds for the small hardship in the stairwell too. And when the neighbour is the one causing trouble, patience and a calm conversation come first, not retaliation.

Truthfulness (sidq) is no side topic in Islam: “Fear Allah and be with the truthful”, says the Quran, and elsewhere: “speak fitting words”. False testimony is to be shunned in one breath with idol worship — “shun the abomination of idols, and shun false testimony”. The Quran is especially sharp where speech and action fall apart: “Why do you say what you do not do?” A good touchstone comes from the Prophet ﷺ: “Sin is what gnaws in your soul and what you would not like people to find out about.” Whoever has lied once puts it right by setting the matter straight, asking for forgiveness, and next time keeping silent rather than glossing over.

Ghiba means saying something about an absent person that he would not like to hear — even when it is true. The Quran compares that with a drastic image: “do not backbite one another. Would any of you like to eat the flesh of his brother when he is dead?” In the same context stand the prohibition of spying on others, of bad assumptions, and of mocking others. The remedy is simple and hard at once: “Whoever believes in Allah and the Last Day, let him speak good or stay silent.” Whoever knows the faults of another covers them — “whoever conceals the faults of a Muslim, Allah conceals his faults in this world and the next”. Not backbiting does not mean silence at any price: warning about a real danger, giving counsel, and reporting a wrong to the responsible authority are something other than gossip.

A man asked the Prophet ﷺ for a piece of advice. He said: “Do not become angry.” The questioner asked several more times — and each time the same answer came. The Quran praises the believers “who restrain their rage and pardon people”, and those who “when they are angry, still forgive”. In practice it helps to first speak the formula of refuge — “A'udhu billahi minash-shaitanir-rajim” — “I seek refuge with Allah from the accursed Satan” —, then to stay silent, leave the room, take some water, and only speak once the pulse is down again. And then the most beautiful advice of the Quran applies: “Repel the evil deed with one that is better, and the one between whom and you there was enmity will become as though he were a warm-hearted friend.”

eintraege.titel: Envy (hasad) and how to dissolve it
eintraege.text: Envy means begrudging another person what Allah has given him. The Quran even has us seek refuge “from the evil of every envier when he envies”, and it makes clear: “Do not wish for that by which Allah has favoured some of you over others… And ask Allah for something of His bounty.” The Prophet ﷺ said briefly and plainly: “Do not envy one another… but be, O servants of Allah, brothers.” The way out is not to suppress feelings but to turn them around: to ask blessing for the other person (“Ma sha Allah, Allahumma barik”), to count your own good, and to ask Allah for more — His store does not run short when someone else receives. And one measure stands: only whoever loves for his brother what he loves for himself truly believes.

Arrogance means rejecting the truth and thinking little of people. The Quran describes it very vividly: “Do not turn your cheek away from people in scorn and do not walk about the earth in insolence, for Allah loves no one who is conceited and boastful” — and soberly: “You will surely not tear open the earth, nor reach the mountains in height.” The abode of the Hereafter is meant for those who “desire neither haughtiness on the earth nor corruption”. The Prophet ﷺ pointed three times at his chest and said: “Piety is here” — rank is not measured by origin, money or looks. Whoever notices that he inwardly looks down on others has already taken the first step; the second is to greet those same people, to listen to them and to do them some good.

tags: why is this happening to me
eintraege.text: Sabr is more than gritting your teeth: staying firm in obedience, staying firm against what is forbidden, and staying calm when something hurts. The Quran announces trials openly — “with something of fear and hunger and loss of property, of lives and of fruits” — and hands those who endure the words straight away: “We belong to Allah, and to Him we return.” For them there are “blessings from their Lord and mercy”, and their reward will come “in full measure, without reckoning”. In practice, what the Quran places alongside it helps: “Seek help in steadfastness and in prayer! Allah is with those who are steadfast.” Patience does not mean doing nothing or accepting injustice — you may complain, weep, ask for help and act; what counts is not losing trust in Allah while doing so.

Shukr means recognising Allah's gifts, saying them out loud and using them rightly. Allah ties a promise to it: “If you are grateful, I will surely give you more.” And He says: “Remember Me, I will remember you. Be grateful to Me and do not be ungrateful towards Me.” That we never come to the end of it is stated explicitly: “If you wanted to count Allah's favours, you could not enumerate them.” In everyday life the word for it is “Alhamdulillah” — “All praise belongs to Allah”; for something joyful it is reported: “Alhamdu lillahil-ladhi bi ni'matihi tatimmus-salihat” — “All praise belongs to Allah, by whose grace good works are completed”. The Prophet ﷺ said that “Alhamdulillah” fills the scale — a word that costs nothing and weighs much.

Tawakkul means: take hold of the means and leave the outcome to Allah. The Quran says it in this order: “And once you have taken a decision, then put your trust in Allah. Truly, Allah loves those who put their trust in Him” — so first plan, work, get treatment, and then let the heart let go. The pledge is great: “Whoever puts his trust in Allah, He is sufficient for him.” The fitting words for it are “Hasbunallahu wa ni'mal-wakil” — “Allah is sufficient for us, and He is the best disposer of affairs” — and “Hasbiyallahu la ilaha illa huwa, alaihi tawakkaltu wa huwa Rabbul-'arshil-'azim” — “Allah is sufficient for me. There is no god but Him. In Him I put my trust, and He is the Lord of the mighty Throne”. The Prophet ﷺ summed it up for Ibn Abbas like this: “When you ask, ask Allah; when you seek help, seek help from Allah.”

The Quran draws a very concrete picture of the modest: “The servants of the Most Gracious are those who walk upon the earth with measured step and who, when the ignorant address them, say: Peace!” Luqman advises his son the same thing in everyday format: do not turn your cheek away in scorn, do not walk in insolence, keep the right measure in your walk and lower your voice. Modesty is not making yourself small: you may achieve good things, have success and be glad about it — only not place yourself above others. The Prophet ﷺ gave a man who wanted to be loved by Allah and by people this advice: “Renounce the world, and Allah will love you; and renounce what is in people's hands, and people will love you.” Whoever compares less, lives more lightly.

The Quran makes reconciliation a task of the community, not only of those quarrelling: “The believers are but brothers. So make peace between your two brothers.” Whoever mediates between people does something good: in many private conversations there is no good, “except in the case of those who enjoin charity, what is right, or reconciliation among people”. You may repay at most in equal measure — “but whoever pardons and brings improvement, his reward lies with Allah”. And the Quran asks a question that unhinges every grudge: “Do you yourselves not love that Allah should forgive you?” The Prophet ﷺ forbade turning away from one another and hating one another. In practice that means: greet first, take the first step, admit your own share — and when a conversation is no longer possible, at least release the other person in your heart and in supplication.

The principle stands clearly in the Quran: “Allah does not forbid you from being kind and just towards those who have not fought you because of religion and have not driven you out of your homes. Truly, Allah loves the just.” Faith cannot be forced — “There is no compulsion in religion” —, and whoever speaks about Islam does so “with wisdom and fair admonition” and argues “in the best way”. Even insulting what others believe is forbidden, so that out of ignorance no insult comes back. Justice applies even towards someone you dislike: “Do not let the hatred you bear against certain people lead you to act unjustly.” Neighbourliness, hospitality, collegiality, caring for sick relatives — none of this knows a religious boundary; the measure with Allah is God-consciousness, not origin.

The Quran does not see animals as objects: “There is no creature on the earth and no bird that flies with its wings but that they are communities like you.” The Prophet ﷺ said: “Allah has prescribed excellence in all things” — and named explicitly that when slaughtering you sharpen the blade and spare the animal suffering. For dealing with creation, moderation applies: “Eat and drink, but be not excessive! He does not love the excessive.” The Quran even names the connection between human action and damage on land and at sea. Very practically, even small things count: removing an obstacle from the path is Sadaqah — handling rubbish, water, electricity and food carefully belongs exactly there.
belege: an-Nawawī Nr. 26 — Sahih al-Buchari, Sahih Muslim

eintraege.text: Work is no opposite of piety in Islam: “When the prayer is finished, then disperse in the land and seek something of Allah's bounty. And remember Allah much.” It has to be honest: “Woe to those who give short measure, who, when they take by measure from people, take in full, but when they measure out or weigh for them, cause loss.” Put positively: “Give full measure when you measure, and weigh with the correct balance.” Wealth may not be acquired “in a vain way”, but through trade by mutual consent; taking interest is forbidden, selling is permitted. The Prophet ﷺ made clear that unlawful income even blocks the supplication, and advised avoiding what is doubtful in order to keep religion and honour pure. On concrete questions of contracts, finance or profession — about loans or insurance, for instance — ask knowledgeable scholars instead of relying on a blanket answer.

eintraege.titel: Using time and small steady deeds
eintraege.text: Surah Al-Asr swears by time and states: “Humankind is truly in loss” — except those who believe, act righteously and enjoin upon one another truth and steadfastness. Time is thereby the capital with which we work. The Prophet ﷺ took Ibn Umar by the shoulder and said: “Be in this world as though you were a stranger or a wayfarer” — and Ibn Umar added: “Take from your health for your illness, and from your life for your death.” The Quran sets the rhythm for it: “So when you have finished, then exert yourself, and towards your Lord direct your longing.” In practice that means: small, firm habits instead of grand resolutions — two pages of Quran daily, one dhikr after the prayer, one Sadaqah a week. Constancy beats intensity, because it carries the day even when motivation wavers.

Allah is the proper name of God in Arabic — Arabic-speaking Christians and Jews use the same word. He is the one, single God: the Creator and Sustainer of all the worlds, without partner, without child, without beginning and without end. Nothing is like Him, and no one but Him deserves worship. Surah 112 (Al-Ikhlas) sums this up in four verses: “He is Allah, One, Allah, the Self-Sufficient. He has not begotten and has not been begotten, and no one is ever equal to Him.” The Quran describes Him with names and attributes — the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful, the All-Knowing, the Forgiving — which show how a Muslim stands towards Him: in awe and at the same time in hope.

Tawhid means recognising Allah as the One — in His lordship, in His worship, and in His names and attributes. In practice that means: Allah alone has created and directs everything; worship, prayer, supplication, sacrifice and trust belong to Him alone; and His names and attributes are accepted as He has described them, without comparing Him with the creation. Tawhid is the core of the Shahada “There is no god but Allah” and the thread running through the whole Quran.

Shirk is the opposite of Tawhid: placing someone or something at Allah's side in what belongs to Him alone — for instance worshipping a created being, calling upon it, ascribing to it power over benefit and harm. The Quran calls Shirk the gravest sin, because it inverts the relationship between the human being and the Creator. Scholars distinguish between major shirk (worshipping another alongside Allah) and hidden minor shirk, such as putting piety on display. Whoever sincerely repents of shirk and turns to Allah finds the door of forgiveness open.

Iman rests on six foundations: belief in Allah, in His angels, in His revealed books, in His messengers, in the Last Day, and in the divine decree — the good as well as the hard. That is how the Prophet ﷺ answered in the well-known Hadith of Jibril, when a stranger in radiantly white clothes asked him about iman. These six form the worldview of a Muslim: where everything comes from, who has sent guidance, where it is all going — and that nothing happens without Allah's knowledge.

In the Hadith of Jibril the Prophet ﷺ explains the three levels of the religion. Islam is the outward action: the five pillars. Iman is the inner conviction: the six articles of faith. Ihsan is the completion of both: “That you worship Allah as though you see Him; for even if you do not see Him, He surely sees you.” Ihsan turns the fulfilment of a duty into a conscious relationship — the same action, only with a wakeful heart.

Angels are creatures of Allah made of light. They have no free will to disobey, but carry out what they are commanded. Well known are Jibril (Gabriel), who brought the revelation to the prophets; Mikail, who is entrusted with rain and provision; Israfil, who will blow the horn; and the Angel of Death, who takes the souls. Further angels record the deeds of people and carry the Throne. To believe in them is one of the six foundations of faith — their exact number is known to Allah alone.

The Quran names several scriptures that Allah has sent down: the Tawrat to Musa (Moses), the Zabur to Dawud (David), the Injil to Isa (Jesus) — and as the final revelation the Quran to Muhammad ﷺ. To believe in all of them is part of the six articles of faith. At the same time Muslims believe that the Quran alone has been preserved unchanged in its wording; Allah Himself has pledged its preservation.

Allah has sent a warner to every people — from Adam, the first human being and prophet, to Muhammad ﷺ, the last. Twenty-five prophets are mentioned by name in the Quran, among them Nuh (Noah), Ibrahim (Abraham), Musa (Moses), Isa (Jesus) and Muhammad ﷺ. Five of them are called Ulu al-Azm, “those of firm resolve”: Nuh, Ibrahim, Musa, Isa and Muhammad ﷺ. All of them called to the same message: to serve Allah alone. No prophet is placed above another in order to belittle another; Muslims believe in them all.

The last prophet is Muhammad ﷺ. The Quran explicitly calls him “the Seal of the Prophets”: “Muhammad is not the father of any of your men, but the Messenger of Allah and the Seal of the Prophets.” After him no further prophet comes. He was born around 570 CE in Mecca, received the first revelation at the age of forty and proclaimed the message for twenty-three years, until his death in Medina. The Quran describes his mission with a single phrase: “And We have sent you only as a mercy for all the worlds.”

eintraege.titel: The Day of Judgement and the life after it
eintraege.text: Muslims believe that this life is a test and that every human being will be raised again after death and called to account. Between death and resurrection lies the Barzakh, the intermediate world of the grave. On the Day of Judgement the horn will be blown, people will be gathered, their books will be handed to them and their deeds will be weighed — and no one is wronged, not even by as much as the weight of a speck of dust. After that comes the eternal life: Paradise for the believers, the Fire for those who turned away. The exact hour is known to Allah alone.

Paradise (Jannah) is the reward for those who believed and did good: gardens beneath which rivers flow, in which they remain forever — and, greater than everything else, the pleasure of Allah. Hell is the warning against the opposite path. The Quran mostly speaks of both in the same breath, so that a person lives between hope and awe and loses neither of the two. Whoever dies as a believer does not, according to Islamic teaching, remain forever in the Fire; the last word belongs to Allah's mercy, which surpasses His wrath.

To believe in the divine decree means: Allah knows everything that was, is and will be, and nothing happens outside His will. That does not cancel a person's responsibility — he chooses and acts, and he is asked about exactly that. The Prophet ﷺ held both together: “Tie your camel and put your trust in Allah.” Belief in Qadar takes the strength out of fear and envy: what has struck you could not have missed you, and what has missed you could not have struck you.

eintraege.titel: The Shahada — the testimony of faith
eintraege.text: The Shahada is: “Ashhadu an la ilaha illa Allah, wa ashhadu anna Muhammadan rasulullah” — “I bear witness that there is no god but Allah, and I bear witness that Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah.” It is the first of the five pillars and the foundation on which all the others rest. Its first part settles to whom worship belongs; its second part settles the way in which worship happens — the way of the Prophet ﷺ.

You become a Muslim by pronouncing the Shahada with conviction: “Ashhadu an la ilaha illa Allah, wa ashhadu anna Muhammadan rasulullah.” No authority and no ceremony is needed for it; witnesses are good but not a condition. After that come the practical steps: ghusl (a full-body washing) as a fresh start, learning wudu and the prayer, and step by step everything else. Islam wipes out what came before — nobody enters carrying an old burden. A good way is to introduce yourself at a local mosque and to let someone accompany you while you learn.

Islam rests on five pillars: first the testimony of faith (Shahada) that there is no god but Allah and Muhammad is His Messenger; second the performance of the five daily prayers; third the payment of Zakat, the obligatory due on wealth; fourth fasting in the month of Ramadan; and fifth the pilgrimage to Mecca (Hajj), once in a lifetime, for whoever is able to do it. That is how the Prophet ﷺ listed them. The Shahada is the foundation, the other four are the load-bearing pillars standing on it.

A Muslim prays five times in every day and night. The five obligatory prayers are called, in the order of the day: Fajr (the morning prayer, from dawn until sunrise), Dhuhr (the midday prayer, from the moment the sun has passed its highest point), Asr (the afternoon prayer, when the shadow grows noticeably longer, until sunset), Maghrib (the evening prayer, directly after sunset) and Isha (the night prayer, after the red evening glow has vanished, until dawn). Every prayer has a time window, not a rigid clock time — which is why the times shift with place and season. Salati calculates them automatically for your location.

Fajr is the first of the five obligatory prayers. Its time begins with the true dawn — the first horizontal strip of light on the horizon — and ends at sunrise. Fajr has two rak'ah of obligatory prayer; before it there are two rak'ah of Sunnah prayer, which the Prophet ﷺ emphasised in particular. It is the prayer that costs the most effort to get up for and therefore weighs especially heavily: the Quran explicitly names the recitation at dawn, because it is witnessed.

Dhuhr is the midday prayer. Its time begins as soon as the sun has passed its highest point and the shadow grows longer again, and it ends when the time of Asr begins. Dhuhr has four rak'ah of obligatory prayer. On Friday, for men in the congregation, the Friday prayer (Jumu'ah) with two rak'ah and a sermon takes its place.

Asr is the afternoon prayer with four rak'ah of obligatory prayer. Its time begins when the shadow of an object has grown noticeably beyond its midday length — the schools of law set the beginning somewhat differently — and it ends at sunset. The Quran urges particular care with the “middle prayer”; many scholars understand this to be Asr, because it falls right in the busiest part of the day.

Maghrib is the evening prayer with three rak'ah of obligatory prayer. Its time begins immediately after sunset and lasts until the red evening glow on the horizon has vanished — a comparatively short window, which is why it is performed promptly after the call to prayer. In Ramadan the breaking of the fast (Iftar) falls exactly on the beginning of the Maghrib time.

Isha is the night prayer, the last of the five obligatory prayers of the day, with four rak'ah of obligatory prayer. Its time begins when the red evening glow after Maghrib has vanished and reaches until the break of dawn; it should, however, be performed before midnight if at all possible. After Isha many follow with the Witr prayer as the close of the night. In northern countries the night in summer can be so short that the Isha time begins very late — for this Salati has calculation methods for high latitudes.

eintraege.titel: How many rak'ah each prayer has
eintraege.text: The obligatory portions (fard) are: Fajr two rak'ah, Dhuhr four, Asr four, Maghrib three and Isha four. In addition there are the emphasised Sunnah prayers, whose counting differs slightly from one school of law to another; by the widespread Hanafi counting they are two before Fajr, four before and two after Dhuhr, two after Maghrib and two after Isha, plus the Witr. Non-emphasised but recommended Sunnah rak'ah exist in addition before Asr and before Isha — four each by the Hanafi counting. Whoever is just starting concentrates first on the fard rak'ah — they are the obligation, everything else comes on top of them.

A prayer begins with the intention in the heart and the takbir “Allahu akbar”, with the hands raised. Standing, the Fatihah is recited, after it a further passage from the Quran. There follows the bowing (ruku) with “Subhana Rabbiyal Azim”, then straightening up with “Sami' Allahu liman hamidah — Rabbana lakal hamd”, then two prostrations (sujud) with “Subhana Rabbiyal A'la”, with a short sitting in between. That is one rak'ah; it is repeated according to the prayer. At the end, seated, follow the Tashahhud and the blessing upon the Prophet ﷺ, then the greeting to the right and to the left: “As-salamu alaikum wa rahmatullah.”

eintraege.titel: What you say in the prayer
tags: what do i say in the prayer
eintraege.text: In the bowing (ruku) you say three times “Subhana Rabbiyal Azim” — “Glory be to my Lord, the Magnificent”. On straightening up the one praying says “Sami' Allahu liman hamidah” and answers himself with “Rabbana wa lakal hamd”. In the prostration (sujud) you say three times “Subhana Rabbiyal A'la” — “Glory be to my Lord, the Most High”; that is the moment in which a human being is closest to Allah, and a good place for a personal supplication. Between the two prostrations you say “Rabbighfir li” — “My Lord, forgive me”.

Al-Fatihah, “the Opening”, is the first Surah of the Quran and has seven verses. It is recited in every rak'ah of every prayer — no prayer is complete without it. Its content is a conversation: first praise and thanks to Allah, the Lord of the worlds, the Most Gracious, the Master of the Day of Judgement; then the declaration “You alone we worship, and You alone we ask for help”; and finally the request that opens up the rest of the Quran: “Guide us on the straight path.”

eintraege.titel: The Qibla — the direction of prayer
eintraege.text: The Qibla is the direction of prayer: towards the Kaaba in Mecca. In the beginning the Muslims prayed towards Jerusalem; then came the command to turn towards the Sacred Mosque — “So turn your face in the direction of the Sacred Mosque.” Whoever does not know the direction for certain makes an effort to the best of their knowledge; a prayer in a direction determined in good faith is valid. Salati shows the Qibla by compass and on a map.

eintraege.titel: The Adhan — the call to prayer
eintraege.text: The Adhan is the call that announces the beginning of a prayer time. It was introduced in Medina after the community had considered how the call to prayer should be given — with a bell, a horn or a fire — and Bilal ﷺ became the first muezzin. Its text professes the greatness of Allah, the Shahada, and the call to prayer and to success. At Fajr the sentence “The prayer is better than sleep” is added. Immediately before the prayer begins, the shorter Iqama follows. Whoever hears the Adhan repeats it quietly along with it and afterwards speaks the blessing upon the Prophet ﷺ.

The Friday prayer replaces the Dhuhr prayer on Friday: two rak'ah in congregation, preceded by the Khutbah (sermon). For adult, resident men it is obligatory; for women, travellers and the sick it is not obligatory, but taking part is permitted and meritorious. The Quran calls on believers to leave trade lying at the call to the Friday prayer and to hurry to the remembrance of Allah. Recommended are ghusl, clean clothes, a pleasant scent, coming early — and staying silent during the Khutbah.

Witr means “odd” and is the prayer with which the night is closed — with an odd number of rak'ah, mostly three, at least one. Its time lies after Isha and reaches until dawn. The schools of law assess it differently: in the Hanafi school it counts as necessary (wajib), in the others as a strongly emphasised Sunnah. The Prophet ﷺ never left it out, neither at home nor while travelling.

Besides the obligatory prayers there are voluntary prayers that supplement the obligatory part and make up for gaps: the emphasised Sunnah prayers around the five times, the Duha prayer in the forenoon, the Tahajjud in the second half of the night, and the Witr. They are not an obligation — whoever leaves them does not sin. The Prophet ﷺ recommended performing voluntary prayers at home, so that the home does not become a place without prayer.

Whoever sleeps through a prayer or forgets it makes it up as soon as he thinks of it — the Prophet ﷺ said: “Whoever forgets a prayer should pray it as soon as he remembers it; there is no other expiation for it.” Whoever leaves it out on purpose commits a serious negligence, but should likewise make it up and repent sincerely. More important than settling the score of old omissions is to build a habit from today onwards that will carry; where many prayers are outstanding, a realistic plan helps more than a perfect one.

On a journey a Muslim may shorten the four-unit obligatory prayers — Dhuhr, Asr and Isha — to two rak'ah each (Qasr); Fajr and Maghrib stay unchanged. The Quran permits this explicitly, and the Prophet ﷺ kept to it on all his journeys. Many scholars additionally allow combining Dhuhr with Asr and Maghrib with Isha. From what distance onwards, and for how long, a journey counts as such is assessed differently by the schools of law — for that it is best to ask your own community or a scholar.

Whoever cannot stand prays while sitting; whoever cannot sit prays lying down and indicates the bowing and the prostration with movements of the head. The prayer does not fall away because of illness, it is only adapted to what is possible — Allah asks of no one more than he is able to give. The purification is eased as well: where water would do harm or is not there, tayammum takes its place.

No prayer without wudu. The steps in order: 1. Form the intention and say “Bismillah”. 2. Wash both hands up to the wrists, three times. 3. Rinse the mouth, three times. 4. Draw water into the nose and blow the nose, three times. 5. Wash the face, three times. 6. Wash the arms up to and including the elbows, right before left, three times each. 7. With wet hands wipe once over the head and wipe out the ears as well. 8. Wash the feet up to and including the ankles, right before left, three times each. 9. To finish, say the Shahada. The washing is always right before left. Obligatory are the face, the arms, wiping the head and the feet; the repetitions are Sunnah.

The wudu becomes invalid, among other things, through everything that leaves the body by the natural way — urine, stool, wind —, through deep sleep while lying down, through unconsciousness, and through heavier bleeding or vomiting (the schools of law assess the latter differently). Mere doubt is not enough: whoever was certain of having wudu and is only unsure whether he has lost it stays with the certainty. After sexual intercourse, after ejaculation, and after the end of menstruation or postnatal bleeding, the full-body washing (ghusl) is required instead of wudu.

Ghusl is the complete washing of the whole body. It becomes obligatory after sexual intercourse or ejaculation as well as after the end of menstruation and postnatal bleeding; it is recommended, among other occasions, before the Friday prayer, before the Eid prayers and when accepting Islam. The procedure: form the intention and say “Bismillah”; wash the hands and the private parts; then a complete wudu; pour water over the head three times and wet the roots of the hair through; then wash the whole body, right before left, so that no spot stays dry.

When no water is available or using it would harm the body, tayammum takes the place of wudu and ghusl: you form the intention, strike both palms on clean earth and wipe with them over the face and afterwards over the arms. How often one strikes and how far one wipes is answered differently by the schools of law — the Hanafi and the Shafi'i school teach two strikes and wiping up to and including the elbows, the Maliki and the Hanbali school one strike and wiping up to the wrists. The Quran permits this explicitly for the sick, for travellers and for everyone who finds no water. As soon as water is available again or is no longer harmful, the normal washing applies once more.

Zakat is the yearly obligatory due on wealth and the third pillar of Islam. Whoever owns wealth above the nisab value (traditionally equated with 85 grams of gold or 595 grams of silver) for a full lunar year gives 2.5 percent of it. Affected are savings, gold, silver, trade goods and the like — not the home you live in yourself or everyday objects. The Quran names prayer and Zakat almost always in one breath: the one sets right the relationship with Allah, the other the relationship with people. For your own calculation it is worth asking at a local Zakat office.

The Quran names eight groups who are entitled to Zakat: the poor and the needy, those employed with it (the administration), those whose hearts are to be won over, for the freeing of slaves, the debtors, for the way of Allah, and the traveller in need. Zakat is therefore not a general donation budget but an earmarked entitlement. It is not given to your own parents, children or spouse — for them there is a duty of maintenance anyway.

Sadaqah is the voluntary gift — at any time, in any amount, to anyone. It is not limited to money: the Prophet ﷺ counted a smile, a good word, the removal of an obstacle from the path and even refraining from what is bad as Sadaqah too. Especially recommended is the ongoing Sadaqah (Sadaqah Jariyah), whose benefit keeps running on — a well, a book, knowledge that is passed on.

To fast in the month of Ramadan is the fourth pillar of Islam. The fast is kept from dawn until sunset: no food, no drink, no marital intercourse — and likewise keeping the tongue and the gaze in check. At the start stands the intention, at the end the breaking of the fast (Iftar), traditionally with dates and water, and before it the meal before dawn (Suhoor). The Quran names the aim of fasting explicitly: “so that you may become God-fearing”.

eintraege.titel: Who does not have to fast
eintraege.text: Whoever is ill or travelling fasts the missed days later — the Quran says this explicitly. The same applies to women during menstruation and postnatal bleeding; they make the days up. Pregnant and breastfeeding women who fear for themselves or for the child may leave off and make up later. Whoever cannot fast permanently, for example because of a chronic illness or advanced age, instead feeds a needy person for every day (fidya). Children do not have to fast; they are only gently brought towards it.

The fast is broken by deliberate eating and drinking, by marital intercourse and by deliberate vomiting. Whoever eats or drinks out of forgetfulness simply carries the fast on — the Prophet ﷺ said that Allah had fed him and given him drink. Brushing the teeth, showering, an injection for treatment or having blood taken do not break the fast according to the widespread view. What stays important: fasting is more than doing without food — whoever does not leave off lying and quarrelling is missing its actual meaning.

Besides Ramadan there are recommended days of fasting: Mondays and Thursdays, the three white days in the middle of every lunar month, the day of Ashura (10 Muharram) and the day of Arafah (9 Dhul-Hijjah) for those who are not on pilgrimage, plus six days in the month of Shawwal after Ramadan. All of them are voluntary — they are an offer, not a yardstick. Fasting on the two Eid days, by contrast, is explicitly forbidden.

eintraege.titel: Laylat al-Qadr — the Night of Decree
eintraege.text: The Night of Decree lies within the last ten nights of Ramadan; the Prophet ﷺ advised looking for it especially in the odd-numbered nights. The Quran says about it: “The Night of Decree is better than a thousand months” — in it the Quran was sent down, and the angels descend until the morning breaks. A supplication reported for this night is: “Allahumma innaka afuwwun tuhibbul afwa fa'fu anni” — “O Allah, You are forgiving and love forgiveness, so forgive me.”

The Hajj is the pilgrimage to Mecca and the fifth pillar of Islam — obligatory once in a lifetime for whoever is physically and financially able to do it. It takes place in the first days of the month of Dhul-Hijjah. The main steps: putting on the ihram together with the intention, the circling of the Kaaba (Tawaf), the walking between Safa and Marwa (Sa'y), the standing on the plain of Arafah on 9 Dhul-Hijjah — the core of the Hajj —, the night in Muzdalifah, the stoning of the pillars in Mina, the sacrifice, and the shortening or shaving of the hair. The Umrah comprises ihram, Tawaf, Sa'y and the shortening or shaving of the hair and can be performed all year round.

In Islam there are two festivals. Eid al-Fitr, the festival of breaking the fast, follows immediately after Ramadan; before the festival prayer the Zakat al-Fitr is paid, a small due for every member of the household, so that even the poorest can celebrate along with everyone. Eid al-Adha, the festival of sacrifice, falls on 10 Dhul-Hijjah, right in the middle of the days of the Hajj, and recalls the readiness of Ibrahim. Both festivals begin with the Eid prayer in congregation, usually in the forenoon, followed by a sermon. On these two days there is no fasting.

eintraege.titel: How an Islamic marriage is concluded
eintraege.text: The Nikah is a contract, not a sacrament, and comes about with few components: the offer and the acceptance in the same sitting, the free consent of both sides, the bridal gift (Mahr) for the bride, and witnesses. According to the majority of the schools of law the bride is represented by her wali, usually the father or a close male relative; the Hanafi school lets an adult woman marry validly even without a wali, but recommends involving him. The schools of law differ on the witnesses: the Hanafi school accepts two men or one man and two women, the Shafi'i and Hanbali schools require two male witnesses, and in the Maliki school the public announcement (i'lan) is what matters most. A short address (Khutbah), the reading out of the contract and a celebration (Walima) belong to the custom, but are not a condition of validity. An imam is not prescribed, but is usual in practice. Important in Germany: the Nikah does not establish a marriage recognised by the state — for residence status, inheritance and custody the civil marriage at the registry office is necessary; scholars and communities therefore urgently advise doing both.
