eintraege.text: The Mahr is the groom's gift to the bride — her personal property, not her family's, and not the price for the marriage. The Quran calls it a gift and expressly leaves it up to her to remit part of it. There is no fixed amount: very small gifts are reported just as much as larger ones, and the Sunnah recommends keeping it easy — the less complicated, the more blessed the marriage. It can consist of money, gold, jewellery, the furnishing of a home, or something immaterial, such as teaching the Quran. Customary is the division into a part due immediately and a deferred part that falls due on divorce or death; both belong in the contract, so that it can be proven later. Because German courts may treat the Mahr as a contractual obligation, a written and clearly quantified wording is worthwhile.

eintraege.titel: Divorce in Islam — talaq, khul and iddah
tags: can a woman ask for divorce
eintraege.text: A separation is permitted, but counts as the very last resort; before it the Quran expressly orders an attempt at arbitration through one person of trust from each of the two families. If the husband dissolves the marriage, that is called talaq; it is revocable twice, after that it is final. The wife for her part can dissolve it: through khul, in which she as a rule gives the Mahr back, or through a judge or an arbitration body if the husband does not consent or violates his duties. Then follows the waiting period (iddah) of three cycles, in the case of pregnancy until the birth; during this time the wife stays provided for and living in the home, and a reconciliation is possible without a new contract. For that whole time the Quran urges decent conduct — “keeping in a lawful manner or releasing in a proper manner”. In Germany the civil divorce must take place in addition; the religious one alone has no effect in state law.

tags: what to do after the birth
eintraege.text: A few transmitted customs belong to a birth, and all of them are simple. Widespread is to speak the call to prayer quietly into the newborn's right ear, so that the first words are the testimony to Allah; the reports about this are rated with differing strength by scholars, but it has never done harm. On the seventh day the child is given its name, the hair of the head is shaved where possible and its weight is donated in silver; also on the seventh day the Aqiqah is customary — a sacrifice, classically two animals for a boy and one for a girl, whose meat is shared with family, neighbours and the needy. It counts as an emphatic Sunnah, not as an obligation, and may be made up later. The name should have a good meaning; the child is named after its father. For the mother the nifas ruling applies, and the Quran names two years as the full period of breastfeeding.

To take in a child, provide for it and bring it up is held in high regard in Islam — it is reported that the one who cares for an orphan will be as near to the Prophet ﷺ in Paradise as two fingers side by side. What the Quran rules out is not the care but the blurring of origin: adopted children are not declared to be biological children, but are named after their fathers; where these are unknown, they are brothers and protégés in religion. This form of lasting care while preserving lineage is called kafalah. From it follows in practice: the child does not inherit automatically — the balance is created through a will or through gifts made during one's lifetime — and once it grows up the usual rules of kinship apply, unless a milk relationship exists. In Germany this corresponds more to guardianship and foster care than to full adoption; for the concrete arrangement legal advice and consultation with a scholar are worthwhile.

eintraege.titel: Plural marriage — what the Quran says
eintraege.text: The Quran permits a husband up to four wives — but in the same verse under a condition that restricts it strongly: whoever fears that he will not act justly should marry only one. Justice here means what can be demonstrated: maintenance, housing, time and attention in equal parts. A further verse states that complete equality of affection will not succeed in any case, and warns against leaving a wife hanging in suspense. The permission is expressly not a recommendation and not an obligation; the historical context of the verse is the provision for widows and orphans after the Battle of Uhud. Many Muslim states today tie it to a court approval. In Germany a second civil marriage is forbidden and punishable, a purely religious second marriage has no effect in civil law and leaves the wife without any protection — scholars and communities clearly advise against it here.

tags: how much is zakat al fitr
eintraege.text: Zakat al-Fitr is the due at the end of Ramadan. It falls due for every Muslim woman and every Muslim who, on the evening of the last day of fasting, owns more than their own needs for that day — the head of the family pays for everyone he provides for, including the children and a child that is born even shortly before the festival. It is classically measured in kind: one sa' of the locally usual staple food, such as wheat, rice or dates, which corresponds to roughly 2.5 to 3 kilograms. Many communities therefore state each year a sum of money that corresponds to this value; whether money instead of food in kind is permissible is answered differently by the schools of law — the Hanafi school expressly allows it, others prefer foodstuffs. It is paid before the Eid prayer, so that it fulfils its purpose: that nobody suffers want on the day of the festival. Whoever gives it too late gives it as an ordinary donation and still makes it up. Salati works out the local amount in the Zakat al-Fitr section.

eintraege.titel: Udhiyah — the sacrifice at Eid al-Adha
eintraege.text: The Udhiyah is the sacrifice on the days of the festival of sacrifice, in remembrance of Ibrahim and his son. The Quran makes clear what it is about: neither the meat nor the blood reaches Allah, but the God-consciousness of the one who gives. What is sacrificed is a sheep or a goat for one household, or a share in a cow or a camel that seven people divide between them; the animal must be healthy and have reached a minimum age. The time begins after the Eid prayer on the tenth of Dhul-Hijjah; how far it reaches is answered differently by the schools of law — the Shafi'i school lets it run until sunset on the thirteenth, the Hanafi school until sunset on the twelfth; whoever slaughters before that has ordinary meat, not a sacrifice. Customary is the division into three: one part for your own family, one part for relatives and neighbours, one part for the needy. Whether the Udhiyah is an obligation or an emphatic Sunnah is assessed differently by the schools of law — the Hanafi school sees it as binding for those of means. In Germany most people have it carried out abroad through aid organisations. Whoever intends to sacrifice refrains from cutting hair and nails from the first of Dhul-Hijjah onwards.

eintraege.titel: Khatmah — reading the whole Quran through
tags: how do i finish the quran
eintraege.text: A Khatmah is one complete pass through the Quran. The classic rhythm is the month: the Quran is divided into thirty Juz', and one Juz' a day gives a whole pass in one month — which is why the Khatmah is so widespread in Ramadan. In practice that is around twenty pages a day, divisible into four blocks of five pages each after the prayers; whoever finds that too much takes half a Juz' and needs two months. The Quran itself sets the measure: read what comes easily to you, and reflect on the signs — understanding comes before speed, and a slow reading with a translation is worth more than a rushed pass. It is transmitted as advice not to read the Quran through in less than three days. At the close a supplication is customary. Salati keeps a Khatmah plan with a daily portion, a progress display and a reminder; missed days can be redistributed instead of giving up.

eintraege.titel: Menstruation — prayer, fasting and the Quran
tags: may i pray during my period
eintraege.text: During menstruation (Arabic hayd) the obligatory prayer falls away completely: a woman does not pray in this time and does not make the missed prayers up afterwards either — that is a relief, not a loss. Fasting falls away as well, but is made up later, day for day. Once the bleeding is over, the full-body washing (ghusl) follows, and after that everything starts again as usual. Dhikr, supplications, listening to recitation and studying are permitted the whole time and are expressly recommended — the connection to Allah does not break off. On touching the Arabic mushaf and on reciting aloud from memory the schools of law differ: some allow it without restriction, others only through a cover, a phone or a translation. Whoever wants to know precisely asks a scholar of their own school of law.

tags: how long no prayer after birth
eintraege.text: Nifas is the bleeding after a delivery. For this time the same applies as with menstruation: no obligatory prayer, no fasting, and the prayers are not made up later; missed days of fasting, however, are. As the maximum duration the classical schools of law predominantly name forty days. If the bleeding stops earlier, the woman performs ghusl and takes up prayer and fasting again at once — the forty days are an upper limit, not a waiting period. If it lasts longer, the bleeding counts by the majority opinion as illness-bleeding, and the woman prays again. After a miscarriage the classification depends on how far the pregnancy had progressed; that is a question of the individual case for a scholar. Dhikr, dua and listening to the Quran are permitted the whole time.

eintraege.titel: Making up missed days of fasting
eintraege.text: Days of fasting that were missed because of menstruation, postnatal bleeding, illness or travel are made up day for day — the Quran says explicitly “an equal number of other days”. The days need not follow one another and need not come at once; it makes sense to finish them before the next Ramadan. Many put them on short winter days or combine them with the Mondays and Thursdays that are recommended anyway. Important: make-up days need the intention before dawn. Voluntary fasting such as the six days in Shawwal does not stand in the way of this, but the obligatory days have priority. Whoever can no longer fast at all because of lasting illness or advanced age instead feeds a needy person for each day (fidya). Salati counts the outstanding days in the fasting section.

eintraege.titel: What a woman covers in prayer
tags: what do i wear when praying
eintraege.text: In prayer, according to the majority of scholars, the following applies to a woman: the whole body is covered except the face and the hands. The garment should be opaque and loose enough that the shape of the body is not outlined; hair and neck belong to what is covered. Whether the feet have to be covered is answered differently — the Hanafi school leaves them uncovered, other schools require them covered; with socks you are on the safe side in any case. A special prayer garment is not prescribed, a wide dress with a headscarf is enough. If the scarf slips briefly and is put right again immediately, the prayer is valid by the majority opinion. For men, at least the area from the navel to the knee applies in prayer, plus a covered shoulder where possible. The Quran puts it generally: “Put on your adornment at every place of worship.”

tags: may a woman go to the mosque
where does a woman stand in prayer
eintraege.text: Women may visit the mosque; it is transmitted that the Prophet ﷺ forbade denying the female servants of Allah the mosques. Visiting the mosque is not an obligation for them: the Friday prayer is not obligatory for women, but the prayer of whoever comes counts fully. In the joint prayer the rows of women stand behind the rows of men; in many mosques there is a separate area or a separate floor for this. If a woman prays with her family at home, she places herself behind the one leading the prayer. If several women pray among themselves, one of them leads the prayer, and she stands in the middle of the row while doing so, not in front of it. Praying at home is expressly connected with great reward for women — both are good, neither is a shortcoming. How a particular women's area is arranged is decided by the local community.

eintraege.titel: Pregnancy and breastfeeding — fasting and prayer
tags: do i have to fast when pregnant
eintraege.text: A pregnant or breastfeeding woman may break off the fast if she fears a danger for herself or for the child — the basis is the same relief as for the sick and for travellers. What the compensation looks like is answered differently: some scholars require only the making up of the days, others additionally or instead the feeding of a needy person for each day (fidya). Which opinion applies in your own case is clarified with a scholar; the medical assessment belongs inside this decision. The prayer stays obligatory, but may be adapted physically: whoever cannot stand prays while sitting, whoever cannot kneel indicates the bowing and the prostration with the upper body. After the birth, the same applies for the time of the postnatal bleeding as described under nifas.

Not every bleeding is a menstruation. Bleeding that occurs outside the accustomed cycle or lasts unusually long counts in the language of fiqh as istihadah and is treated like a lasting impairment, not like hayd. That means: prayer and fasting stay obligatory. In practice you proceed by counting the usual cycle days as menstruation and praying normally the rest of the time; for each prayer time the ablution is made anew, after the place has been cleaned and protected. If a little blood comes during that time, it does not make the prayer already begun invalid. Because the distinction depends on the cycle and is tricky in the individual case, consultation with a knowledgeable scholar is worthwhile — and with persistent bleeding a visit to the doctor is called for anyway.

eintraege.titel: Sajdat as-Sahw — when you lose count in the prayer
eintraege.text: Whoever forgets a step in the prayer, prays one rak'ah too many or too few, or is unsure how far along he is, does not have to break the prayer off. For such cases there is the prostration of forgetfulness, Sajdat as-Sahw: two additional prostrations that make up for the mistake. When unsure you assume the smaller number, add the missing rak'ah and afterwards make the two prostrations. Where exactly they belong — before or after the Salam — is answered differently by the schools of law; both ways are attested, and in both cases the prayer is valid. Not every mistake calls for them: a forgotten Sunnah part such as the opening supplication is only made up while you are still at that point. Whoever leaves out an obligatory pillar such as the bowing entirely and notices it only later repeats the rak'ah concerned. The Quran recalls that forgetting is not counted as guilt.

eintraege.titel: Coming late to the congregational prayer (masbuq)
eintraege.text: Whoever comes to the congregational prayer after it has begun is called masbuq and simply joins in where the imam currently is — without making up the missed parts first. You say the takbir standing and follow the movement of the imam at once. As a complete rak'ah counts, by the majority opinion, whoever still reaches the bowing (ruku) together with the imam. After the imam's Salam the masbuq stands up alone and makes up exactly the rak'ah that he is missing; he does the recitation himself while doing so. If you arrive only after the Salam, you pray the prayer alone. What matters is calm: the transmitted advice is to walk at a measured pace and not to run — what you reach you pray along with, what is missing you complete afterwards.

eintraege.titel: Praying on a plane, on a train or in a car
eintraege.text: An obligatory prayer is performed standing and facing the Qibla wherever possible — while travelling too. In practice that means: if a stop is possible, you halt and pray outside the vehicle. If that is not possible, because you are sitting on a plane or in a moving train, you pray while seated and indicate the bowing and the prostration with the upper body, with the prostration going lower than the bowing. You align yourself towards the Qibla at the takbir as far as it goes; if the vehicle changes direction, that does not make the prayer invalid. As the driver you do not pray while driving — safety comes first, the prayer waits until the next stop. While travelling you may also shorten the four-unit prayers and combine Dhuhr with Asr as well as Maghrib with Isha. The Quran expressly permits praying “on foot or riding” when the situation demands it.

eintraege.titel: Prayer and fasting in Northern Europe
eintraege.text: In Northern Europe the sun lies so flat in summer that the evening twilight no longer ends — then there is no astronomical sign for Isha and sometimes none for Fajr either. For this situation scholars have described three recognised ways: take the times of the nearest place that still has a real night; transfer the times of Mecca; or take as a basis the last night of the year in which the signs were still visible (Aqrab al-Ayyam). Salati offers the usual high-latitude procedures for this in the settings — it is a method of calculation, not a question of faith, and the local community usually follows one particular choice. For fasting the same principle applies: where the day practically does not end, you fall back on the times of a comparison city or of Mecca. Whoever reaches their limit health-wise breaks off and makes the days up later — the Quran expressly stresses ease instead of hardship.

eintraege.titel: The sutrah — the screen in front of the one praying
eintraege.text: A sutrah is an object that you place in front of you when praying alone: a wall, a pillar, a chair, a bag, at need the prayer mat as a marker. It shows where your own prayer area ends and invites others to walk around it. The Prophet ﷺ is reported to have prayed in front of a spear or a saddle post and to have stood close enough to it that little room was left. If someone passes by anyway, the prayer does not become invalid through it; you may calmly hold him back with your hand, but you neither break off nor scold. If you pray in congregation, the imam's sutrah serves the whole row — those praying behind him need none of their own. Whether the sutrah is an obligation or an emphatic Sunnah is assessed differently by scholars; the great majority see it as a strong Sunnah.

eintraege.titel: Tahajjud — the prayer in the night
eintraege.text: Tahajjud is the voluntary prayer in the night after you have slept; in the wider sense every prayer at night is called Qiyam al-Lail. It is not an obligation, but is expressly recommended in the Quran — for the Prophet ﷺ it was an additional distinction. It is prayed in pairs: two rak'ah at a time, as many pairs as you wish, usually two to eight; the night is closed with the Witr. The best time is the last third of the night, shortly before Fajr — it is transmitted that Allah then answers supplications especially closely. Whoever has already prayed the Witr before sleeping still prays Tahajjud and does not repeat the Witr. For beginners the simplest entry helps: get up twenty minutes earlier, pray two rak'ah, speak a personal supplication. Constancy in small things is, by the reports, more beloved than a single long night.

eintraege.titel: The Duha prayer in the forenoon
eintraege.text: The Duha prayer is a voluntary prayer in the forenoon. Its time begins when the sun stands about the length of a spear above the horizon — in practice around twenty minutes after sunrise — and ends shortly before the sun stands at its zenith, that is, before Dhuhr. At least two rak'ah are prayed, usually two to eight, always in pairs with a Salam. It is transmitted that every joint of a human being owes a charity each day and that the two rak'ah of the Duha are enough for it. Because it falls into working and school hours, it is the most frequently forgotten of the recommended prayers; a short break is enough for it. In some regions it is called Chasht or Ishraq — Ishraq more precisely denotes the first minutes after sunrise. Salati can set a reminder for the time window.

eintraege.titel: Tarawih — the night prayer of Ramadan
eintraege.text: Tarawih is the voluntary congregational prayer in the nights of Ramadan, prayed after Isha and closed with the Witr. It is not an obligation, but is emphatically recommended; transmitted is the promise that whoever spends the nights of Ramadan in prayer, in faith and in hope of reward, will be forgiven. On the number of rak'ah there are two widespread traditions: eight rak'ah plus Witr, as transmitted from the practice of the Prophet ﷺ, and twenty rak'ah plus Witr, as has become established in many communities since the time of Umar. Both ways are valid and are held by scholars — the number is not a dispute about right and wrong, but about the measure. It is prayed in pairs with short breaks; hence the name, which goes back to “resting”. Whoever cannot get to the mosque prays at home, alone or with the family.

eintraege.titel: Sajdat at-Tilawah — the prostration when reciting
eintraege.text: At certain places in the Quran the prostration is spoken of; whoever reads or hears such a place prostrates once — that is the Sajdat at-Tilawah. Most editions mark these verses in the margin with a symbol of their own; depending on the counting tradition there are fourteen or fifteen such places, and Salati shows the marker in the reader. The procedure is plain: you say the takbir, prostrate once, speak the usual words of praise there, and straighten up again. An ablution is presupposed by the majority; whether the prostration is an obligation or a recommended Sunnah is answered differently by the schools of law — the Hanafi school sees it as binding, the others as Sunnah. Whoever cannot carry it out at that moment, on the bus for instance, reads on and makes it up later, or says words of praise instead.

eintraege.titel: Wiping over socks and leather footwear (mash)
tags: do i have to wash my feet
eintraege.text: Instead of washing the feet you may wipe over the footwear during wudu — that is the mash over the khuff. The conditions are: you put the footwear on while you were completely pure, it covers the ankles, and it holds up while walking. Whether thin fabric socks are enough is judged differently: some scholars require firm leather or leather-like socks, others allow any durable sock that water does not soak through. You wipe once with wet hands over the top of the foot, not over the sole. The permission lasts for one day and one night, while travelling for three days and nights, counted from the first breaking of wudu after putting them on. It ends when the period runs out or a full-body washing falls due — then the feet are washed again. For your own school of law it is best to ask a scholar.

tags: is jesus the son of god
eintraege.text: Isa, the son of Maryam, is in Islam one of the greatest messengers of Allah and one of the five of firm resolve. The Quran calls him al-Masih, the Messiah, reports of his birth without a father as a sign of Allah, of his miracles by Allah's permission, and of the fact that he brought the Gospel and announced a messenger to come after him. Maryam is the only woman with a whole Surah bearing her name; the Quran calls her chosen and pure above all the women of the world — Muslims honour her to a high degree. The difference from the Christian creed lies at two points: Isa is a servant and messenger of Allah, not the son of God and not part of a trinity; and according to the Quran he was not crucified but raised up to Allah. Whoever does not acknowledge Isa is not a Muslim — belief in all the prophets is part of the six articles of faith.

eintraege.titel: Sunnis and Shia — what is it about?
eintraege.text: The origin of the separation is historical, not theological: after the death of the Prophet ﷺ in the year 632 the question of the succession in the leadership of the community arose. The later Sunni majority recognised the election of Abu Bakr and of the caliphs who followed, while a group spoke out for Ali ibn Abi Talib and his descendants — out of this party (Arabic shia) there grew over time a tradition of its own, with its own Hadith collection, its own legal doctrine and its own days of remembrance. Common to both are the Quran, belief in the one God, in Muhammad ﷺ as Prophet, the prayer, fasting, Zakat and Hajj. Differences show up in the authority of the imams, in details of the prayer and in the assessment of some Companions. The Quran urgently warns to hold fast together to the rope of Allah and not to split apart. Salati follows the Sunni majority tradition in its content and names it where views differ.

The Arabic word jihad means literally exertion or effort, not war — for war Arabic has the word qital. The Quran uses jihad first of all for the exertion on the way of Allah in general: against your own lower inclinations, for knowledge, for justice, with your wealth and with your own person. Where the Quran speaks of armed fighting, it is bound to conditions: it is defence against those who fight, it may not overstep the limits, and non-combatants are protected; when the attack ends, the fighting ends. Expressly it holds: there is no compulsion in religion — forcing people into Islam is prohibited. Terror against civilians contradicts these foundations; the Quran equates the unjustified killing of one human being with the killing of the whole of humankind. Moreover, on questions of war and peace it is not individuals who judge, but recognised scholars and legitimate authorities.

eintraege.titel: Why is the prayer in Arabic?
tags: do i have to know arabic
eintraege.text: The Quran was, by its own statement, sent down as an Arabic Quran; for Muslims it is Allah's word in its very wording, and a translation renders only the meaning. That is why the Arabic text is recited in the prayer — through it Muslims worldwide pray the same words, and a traveller can join any row anywhere. Whoever does not yet know the words is not shut out: you begin with al-Fatihah and a short Surah, speak them at first from the transliteration and learn piece by piece. Supplications outside the fixed recitation may be spoken in any language — Allah understands every heart. Whether a beginner may say the Fatihah in translation for a transitional period is answered differently by the schools of law; all agree that the goal is the Arabic text. Salati offers transliteration, word-by-word translation and listening exercises for this.

The Quran does not pass over suffering in silence but declares it part of the test: death and life are created in order to test who acts best, and the testing comes with bad things as well as with good. Part of it is the pledge that no one is burdened with more than he can carry, and that with hardship comes ease. A second part of the answer lies in the freedom of the human being: much injustice in the world goes back to human decisions, and the task is to stand against it instead of accepting it. The third part is the Hereafter — the balance that this world stays in debt for is settled there; no injustice remains unseen. The Quran promises blessing and guidance to those who stay patient. Whoever loses the ground under their feet may lament: prophets too spoke out their distress before Allah, and that belongs expressly to faith, not against it.

eintraege.titel: What about people who have never heard of Islam?
eintraege.text: The Quran answers this with a clear principle: Allah does not punish before He has sent a messenger; messengers were sent expressly so that people would have no argument against Allah. Whoever demonstrably was never reached by the message in an understandable form therefore does not bear the same responsibility as someone who knew it and rejected it. The classical scholars speak here of the “people of the interval” and mostly assume that they will undergo a test of their own on the Day of Judgement. How it goes for a particular person is decided by none of us: over the fate of individuals in the Hereafter Allah alone judges, and Muslims assign neither Paradise nor Hell to anyone by name. For children who die before maturity it holds, by the majority opinion, that they are not called to account. What remains is our own task: to invite in a friendly way, not to judge.

Tasawwuf, in English mostly called Sufism, denotes the occupation with the inner side of faith: sincerity of intention, cleansing the heart of arrogance, envy and hypocrisy, constant remembrance of Allah. Its classical point of reference is the term ihsan from the Hadith of Jibril — to serve Allah as though you saw Him. In this sense tasawwuf is neither a religion of its own nor a sect, but a field of study alongside aqidah and fiqh, and many great scholars of history were jurists and Sufis at the same time. Over the centuries orders (tariqa) formed, with their own chains of teachers and their own forms of dhikr. Such forms are judged by whether they keep to the Quran and the Sunnah; where practices go beyond that — for instance exaggerated veneration of teachers or of graves — other scholars contradict them clearly. This assessment is a well-known dispute within Islam, not a marginal topic; whoever wants to go deeper should ask knowledgeable scholars.

eintraege.titel: Do I have to change my name as a convert?
tags: do i have to change my name
eintraege.text: No. Whoever accepts Islam does not have to change their name — on the contrary, the Quran expressly states that people are to be named after their fathers; the line of descent therefore stays intact. The surname is not Islamised either. A name is changed only when its meaning contradicts the faith, for instance because it names a lord other than Allah or carries an ugly meaning; the Prophet ﷺ changed individual names in such cases and otherwise left the existing ones as they were. Many converts additionally choose an Arabic name to be called by in the community — that is a free decision, not a requirement, and officially nothing changes through it. A German — or any other non-Arabic — first name is no obstacle to prayer, marriage or burial.

eintraege.titel: What about my life before Islam?
tags: do i have to make up prayers
do i have to make up fasts
eintraege.text: With the acceptance of Islam a fresh start begins: it is transmitted that Islam wipes out everything that lay before it, and the Quran expressly promises forgiveness for the past to those who stop. Prayers, days of fasting or Zakat from the time before the Shahada are therefore not made up — the duties begin with the day of acceptance. What remains are the rights of other people: debts, borrowed items, damage for which you are responsible should still be settled or put right, because they are owed to people, not to Allah. Some converts are tormented by their own past for a long time; against this the verse helps that Allah forgives all sins and that sincere repentance can even exchange bad deeds for good ones. A detailed listing of old sins is neither foreseen nor necessary.

eintraege.titel: How do I tell my non-Muslim family?
tags: how do i tell my parents
eintraege.text: There is no prescribed form and no deadline for this — the timing is a wise weighing-up, not a question of faith. What the Quran sets out is the attitude: parents are still treated with kindness, even when they reject the faith; only a demand to give up the faith is not followed. The invitation is given “with wisdom and fair admonition”, not with quarrelling. In practice this proves itself: first let your own behaviour speak, then in a calm moment explain openly and without technical terms what changes and what does not; fears mostly circle around estrangement, not around theology. Holidays, invitations to meals and caring for parents remain part of life. Where a reaction could become dangerous, it is permitted to stay silent at first. A local community or a circle of converts often gives very practical support in this time.

eintraege.titel: Ghusl and circumcision after the Shahada
tags: what to do after the shahada
eintraege.text: After the acceptance of Islam the full-body washing (ghusl) is carried out. Some scholars hold it to be an obligation, others emphatically recommended — it is transmitted that the Prophet ﷺ instructed new Muslims to perform the washing. It is quickly explained: form the intention, make wudu, wet the whole body thoroughly once with water. Circumcision (khitan) is judged differently in the schools of law: partly as an obligation, partly as a strong Sunnah and part of the natural disposition. For adult converts it is nowhere forced — prayer, fasting, marriage and Hajj are valid without it, and where a medical risk exists it falls away anyway. Whoever considers it clarifies that calmly with a doctor and with a scholar. More important for the beginning are the five prayers, a few Surahs learnt by heart, and connection to a community.

eintraege.titel: May I join in Christmas and birthdays?
eintraege.text: Here a distinction has to be made between the relationship and the act of worship. The Quran expressly does not forbid being kind and just towards people who do not fight you — visits, eating together, gifts and courtesy towards the family therefore remain permitted, and towards parents they are even commanded. The boundary lies where you take part in the religious acts of another faith or say along statements that contradict tawhid. How far taking part in a family meal on 24 December goes beyond that is assessed differently by scholars: some see no problem in merely being together, others advise against everything that counts as celebrating the festival along. Our own Islamic festivals are Eid al-Fitr and Eid al-Adha. Whoever is unsure discusses the concrete family situation with a scholar — blanket answers rarely fit here.

The Quran is the word of Allah, revealed to Muhammad ﷺ over about twenty-three years — not all at once, but bit by bit, fitting the situations of the community. It comprises 114 Surahs; in the widespread Hafs counting there are 6236 verses, while other counting traditions arrive at slightly differing numbers. For reading, the text is additionally divided into 30 equally large sections (Juz') — so the whole Quran can be read through in one Ramadan, for example. A distinction is made between Meccan Surahs, which were revealed before the emigration and mostly speak of tawhid, resurrection and patience, and Medinan Surahs, which order community, law and everyday life more strongly. The first command revealed was “Read in the name of your Lord, who created.”

The Quran was preserved from the beginning in two ways at once: in the memory of the Companions, who learnt it by heart, and in writing, because the Prophet ﷺ had every revelation recorded by scribes and placed in its position. Under Abu Bakr what had been written down was collected, under Uthman it was brought together into one uniform mushaf and sent out to the provinces — this version is the basis of all editions today. To this day there are millions of people worldwide who know the complete text by heart (huffaz), so that a silent alteration would be practically impossible. Allah Himself has pledged this preservation: “Truly, it is We who have sent down the Reminder, and truly, We will be its guardian.”

A Surah is a chapter of the Quran; a verse is called ayah in Arabic — literally “sign”. The Surahs are of very different lengths: Al-Baqarah, the second Surah, has 286 verses, Al-Kawthar only three. Every Surah carries a name that mostly goes back to a striking word or image within it, and it is numbered as well; the usual way of citing is “Surah : verse”, so 2:255 for the Throne Verse. All Surahs except the ninth (At-Tawbah) begin with the Basmala: “Bismillaahi r-Rahmaani r-Rahiim” — “In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.” Whether the Basmala counts in each case as a verse of its own is seen differently by the counting traditions; in the Fatihah it is, in the widespread counting, verse 1.

Before reading you seek refuge with Allah — the Istiadhah “A'udhu billaahi mina sh-shaytaani r-rajiim” —, because the Quran says: “When you recite the Quran, seek refuge with Allah from the outcast Satan.” After that follows the Basmala, unless you start in the middle of Surah 9. It is read in tartil: calmly, in clear units, with the correct lengths and pauses, not rushed — “and recite the Quran in a measured way”. Better a little and attentively than much and fleetingly; whoever is starting out takes short Surahs and reads them aloud, slowly and, if possible, to a teacher. Where someone is reciting, this applies to those listening: listen closely and stay silent.

The Quran was revealed in Arabic — “We have sent it down as an Arabic Quran, so that you may understand” —, and the Arabic wording itself is the Quran. A translation therefore always renders only the meaning, the way a human being has understood it; that is why good editions are called “the approximate meaning of the Quran”. In the prayer the recitation is therefore in Arabic, also by people who do not yet know any Arabic. For understanding, a translation is nevertheless indispensable, best of all together with an explanation (tafsir) that names the context of the verses. A good way is to read both side by side: the Arabic text aloud, the translation silently — and to learn the Arabic step by step.

eintraege.titel: Juz', hizb and rub' — the reading divisions
eintraege.text: Besides Surahs and verses, the Quran is divided into reading sections that make reading it through plannable. The largest unit is the Juz': 30 roughly equally long parts — whoever reads one a day manages the whole Quran in a month. Every Juz' consists of two hizb, every hizb of four quarters (rub'), which are marked in the margin of the page. The best-known section is Juz' Amma, the thirtieth, which contains the short Surahs from the end of the Quran and with which many learners begin. This division is a later reading aid and not part of the revelation — section boundaries therefore sometimes fall in the middle of a Surah.

Ayat al-Kursi is verse 255 of Surah Al-Baqarah and counts as the mightiest verse of the Quran, because it describes in one sweep who Allah is: “Allah — there is no god but Him, the Ever-Living, the Sustainer of all. Neither drowsiness nor sleep overtakes Him.” It goes on to say that everything in the heavens and on the earth belongs to Him, that no one intercedes without His permission, that His knowledge encompasses everything, and that guarding the heavens and the earth does not burden Him. Many Muslims read the verse after every obligatory prayer and before going to sleep; there are well-known reports about this in al-Bukhari and Muslim. It is also one of the first verses that learners memorise.

Al-Ikhlas is the 112th Surah and has only four short verses, in which the core of the Islamic picture of God stands: “Say: He is Allah, One, Allah, the Self-Sufficient. He has not begotten and has not been begotten, and no one is ever equal to Him.” The name means “the sincere devotion” or “the pure turning towards Him” — in four lines the Surah settles to whom worship belongs and to whom it does not. According to a statement of the Prophet ﷺ transmitted in al-Bukhari it weighs a third of the Quran, because it carries its central theme within it. Because of its brevity it is usually the first Surah that children and new Muslims learn by heart, and it is recited in many prayers.

eintraege.titel: Al-Falaq and An-Nas — the two Surahs of refuge
eintraege.text: The last two Surahs of the Quran, Al-Falaq (113) and An-Nas (114), are together called Al-Mu'awwidhataan — “the two Surahs of refuge”. Al-Falaq begins with “Say: I take refuge with the Lord of the daybreak” and then names the evils from which protection is sought: what has been created, the darkness when it falls, sorcery and envy. An-Nas takes refuge with the Lord, King and God of humankind from the whisperer who slinks away — that is, from what attacks from within. Both are read together with Al-Ikhlas three times each in the morning and in the evening and before going to sleep; that too is transmitted in al-Bukhari. They are short enough to be learnt by heart in a few days.

Al-Kawthar is, with three verses, the shortest Surah of the Quran: “Truly, We have given you al-Kawthar. So pray to your Lord and sacrifice. Truly, the one who hates you — he is the one cut off from good.” Al-Kawthar means “the abundance”; scholars explain it as the rich good that Allah gave the Prophet ﷺ, and according to an explanation of the Prophet ﷺ transmitted in Muslim it refers in particular to a river in Paradise. The Surah was revealed at a time when opponents were mocking him as being without descendants and therefore without a future — the answer turns that around. Because of its brevity it is well suited as the second Surah in the prayer.

Ya-Sin is the 36th Surah with 83 verses and is one of the best-known and most frequently recited Surahs of all. It begins with the letters Ya-Sin and an oath by the wise Quran: “you are truly one of the messengers, on a straight path” — the Surah therefore first confirms the mission of the Prophet ﷺ. After that it tells the parable of a town that turned its messengers away, brings signs of creation before the eyes — day and night, sun and moon, the dead land that lives again — and closes with the resurrection. The widespread designation “heart of the Quran” comes from a report whose chain scholars classify as weak; the Surah therefore stays meritorious like every reading of the Quran, without any need to ascribe special effects to it.

Al-Kahf, “the Cave”, is the 18th Surah with 110 verses. It tells four stories that all circle around trials: the young men in the cave (faith), the man with the two gardens (wealth), Musa and al-Khidr (knowledge) and Dhul-Qarnayn (power). Many Muslims read it on Friday; there are reports on this in al-Hakim and al-Bayhaqi according to which a light shines between the two Fridays for whoever reads it on Friday — scholars assess these chains differently, but the habit is widespread and undisputedly good. On its first and last ten verses there is moreover a statement transmitted in Muslim about protection from the trial of the Dajjal. Its closing verse sums up the message: act righteously and associate no one with Allah in serving Him.

Hifz means keeping the Quran in your memory — and the Quran itself pledges: “And We have indeed made the Quran easy to remember.” Four basic principles carry almost every path of learning: first, a little every day instead of a lot rarely, better three verses every day than one page at the weekend; second, read aloud and listen to a correct recitation while doing so, so that the right pronunciation is impressed from the start; third, revision (murajaah) — what has already been learnt needs more time than the new material, otherwise it falls apart; fourth, use what you have learnt in the prayer, because there it settles by itself. It helps to always learn from the same mushaf edition, because the eye remembers the look of the page. And a teacher you recite to finds mistakes that you would never notice yourself.

The Arabic alphabet has 28 letters and is written from right to left. It knows no capital and small letters, but almost every letter changes its shape depending on whether it stands alone or is joined at the beginning, in the middle or at the end of a word. The order is: Alif, Ba, Ta, Tha, Jim, Ha, Kha, Dal, Dhal, Ra, Zay, Sin, Shin, Sad, Dad, Ta, Za, Ain, Ghain, Fa, Qaf, Kaf, Lam, Mim, Nun, Ha, Waw, Ya. Several letters differ only by their dots — Ba, Ta and Tha have the same basic body —, which is why it is worth learning them in groups. The hamza is often counted along as a sound of its own, but traditionally does not count as the 29th letter; Lam-Alif is a writing ligature, not a letter of its own.

Arabic is written in a joined-up script: the letters of a word hang together. Every letter therefore has up to four forms — isolated, at the start of a word, in the middle and at the end. The basic shape stays recognisable in all of them; joined forms are mostly compressed, while the isolated form and the final form keep the full sweep. Six letters join only to the right and never to the left: Alif, Dal, Dhal, Ra, Zay and Waw. If one of them stands in the middle of a word, the line breaks off after it and the next letter starts anew — which is why a word like “Qur'an” looks visually like two pieces. Whoever knows these six can recognise word boundaries in the mushaf far more reliably.

Arabic letters do not carry the short vowels within them; they are set as small marks (harakat) above or below the letter. There are three: the fathah, a slanted stroke above the letter, pronounces it with a short “a”; the kasrah, the same stroke below the letter, gives a short “i”; the dammah, a small waw above the letter, gives a short “u”. Out of the letter Ba you get in this way “ba”, “bi” and “bu”. In ordinary Arabic texts these marks are mostly missing, but in the mushaf every one of them is written — which is why you can read the Quran correctly as soon as you have mastered the letters and the harakat. The short vowels really are spoken short, about half as long as a long vowel; that is the first step towards clean Tajweed.

eintraege.titel: Sukun — the letter without a vowel
eintraege.text: The sukun is a small circle above a letter and means: this letter has no vowel. It is attached directly to the preceding vowelled letter and thereby closes the syllable. In “min” the mim carries a kasrah and the nun a sukun — you say “min” in one sweep, not “mi-na”. A letter with a sukun is called “sakin”, and a word can never begin with a sakin letter. The sukun is the starting point of almost all Tajweed rules: nun sakinah, mim sakinah, Qalqalah and the Madd rules all presuppose that you recognise which letter is vowelless.

The shadda is a small mark like a “w” above a letter and means that this letter is pronounced twice: once vowelless and once with a vowel, in one sweep and with a little more pressure. In “Rabb” (Lord) or “inna” (truly) the doubling is clearly heard. It is not a question of beauty but can change the meaning — a simple and a doubled verb are different words. Together with the shadda an additional vowel mark often stands; fathah and dammah then stand above the shadda, the kasrah mostly below the letter. If nun or mim carry a shadda, the Ghunnah must be held as well, the nasal sound of about two counts.

eintraege.titel: Tanwin — the nunation at the end of a word
eintraege.text: Tanwin means: at the end of a word the vowel mark is doubled, and an “n” is pronounced along with it — written are two fathah, two kasrah or two dammah. Out of “kitaab” you get “kitaabun”, “kitaaban” or “kitaabin”. This attached “n” exists only in the pronunciation, not as the letter nun; in Tajweed, however, it is treated exactly like a nun sakinah, which is why the same rules — Izhar, Idgham, Iqlab, Ikhfa — apply to it. The doubled fathah is mostly set on an alif written in addition. If you stop at the end of the word, the tanwin disappears: at the pause “kitaaban” becomes a long “kitaabaa”, while “kitaabun” and “kitaabin” become simply “kitaab”.

Three letters serve in Arabic as long vowels and are therefore called madd letters. An alif without a vowel of its own after a fathah gives a long “aa”, a vowelless waw after a dammah a long “uu”, a vowelless ya after a kasrah a long “ii”. This combination is what is decisive: only when the preceding vowel matches the letter is there a lengthening — otherwise it is no madd. The basic lengthening is called Madd Tabi'i, the “natural lengthening”, and lasts two counts (harakat), that is, about twice as long as a short vowel. The difference carries meaning: spoken short and spoken long, a word can be two entirely different words, which is why holding the lengths cleanly belongs to the core of reading the Quran.

The basic level is the Madd Tabi'i, the natural lengthening of two counts — everywhere a long vowel stands and no hamza and no sukun follows, for example in “qaala”. If a hamza follows the long vowel within the same word, this is called the Madd Muttasil, the “connected lengthening”, as in “as-samaa'” or “jaa'a”; it is held longer than the natural lengthening, by the widespread Hafs transmission four to five counts, and all ways of reading agree that here a lengthening must be made. If the long vowel stands at the end of a word and the next word begins with a hamza, it is the Madd Munfasil, the “separated lengthening”, for instance in “innaa a'tainaaka”; here the transmissions differ — by Hafs from Aasim four to five counts are mostly read, other ways read shorter. What matters above all is to keep the length once chosen the same throughout the whole recitation.

The Arabic article “al-” is always written the same way, but not always pronounced the same way. Before the 14 moon letters the lam stays audible: “al-qamar” (the moon), “al-kitaab”, “al-hamdu”. Before the 14 sun letters the lam falls silent and the following letter is doubled: written stands “al-shams”, spoken is “ash-shams” (the sun), likewise “ar-Rahmaan” and “as-salaam”. In the mushaf you recognise it at once: with sun letters the letter after the lam carries a shadda, and the lam itself has no sukun. The sun letters are Ta, Tha, Dal, Dhal, Ra, Zay, Sin, Shin, Sad, Dad, Ta, Za, Lam and Nun — all the rest are moon letters.

The Hamzat al-Wasl is a helping sound at the beginning of a word: if you start reading at that point, you pronounce it; if you read straight through from the previous word, it simply falls away. In the mushaf it is recognisable by a small sad-like sign above the alif. Examples are the article “al-” and words such as “ism” — which is why at the start you say “Al-hamdu lillaah”, but in the flow “bismillaah”, without an audible vowel before the “sm”. Which vowel is pronounced when starting anew depends on the word: with the article it is always an “a”, with verbs an “i” or a “u”, for instance “idhhab” and “udkhul”. To be distinguished from it is the Hamzat al-Qat', the firm hamza, which is always pronounced — as in “amana” or “iimaan”.

The Ta Marbutah is a ha with two dots above it and stands only at the end of a word. It mostly marks the feminine form of a word: “muslim” becomes “muslima”, “kabiir” becomes “kabiira”. Its pronunciation depends on whether you read on or stop: if you read through, you pronounce it as a “t” with its vowel — “rahmatun”, “jannatun”; if you stop at the end of the word, it becomes a breathed “h” or falls silent entirely — “rahmah”, “jannah”. That is exactly how, when listening, you can tell whether someone is pausing or connecting. To be distinguished from it is the open ta, which stays a “t” at the pause as well, for instance in “bint”.

Tajweed literally means “to do something well” and denotes the rules for pronouncing every letter of the Quran at its right place and with its right qualities — with the fitting lengths, pauses and nasal sounds. The Quran itself sets the direction: “and recite the Quran in a measured way” (tartil). The rules were not invented but describe how the Prophet ﷺ recited; they have been handed down through an unbroken chain from teacher to student, which is why Tajweed is to this day learnt above all by reciting aloud and being corrected, not from books alone. Scholars distinguish the gross mistake (lahn jali), which distorts the meaning, from the fine mistake (lahn khafi), which only diminishes the beauty; how strictly the latter is to be judged they see differently. Whoever is still at the beginning reads slowly and carries on without fear — the Prophet ﷺ expressly promised reward also to the one who struggles with the Quran.

The makhraj is the place in the mouth and throat where a letter is produced — the basis of every correct recitation, because many Arabic sounds sound similar to English-speaking ears and differ solely by their place. The widespread division according to Ibn al-Jazari knows 17 points of articulation in five areas: the air space of mouth and throat (jawf) for the long vowels, the throat (halq) for hamza and ha, ain and ha, ghain and kha, the tongue (lisaan) with most of the letters, the lips (shafataan) for Ba, Mim, Waw and Fa, and the nasal cavity (khayshum) for the Ghunnah. Other scholars count 16 or 14 places — the pronunciation itself is undisputed here, only the way of counting differs. The best way to learn the makharij is to pronounce a sound without a vowel and to feel where exactly it strikes.

eintraege.titel: Nun sakinah and tanwin — the four rules
eintraege.text: When a vowelless nun or a tanwin meets the next letter, one of four rules applies. Izhar (clear pronunciation) before the six throat letters hamza, ha, ain, ha, ghain and kha — the nun stays clearly audible, as in “an'amta”. Idgham (merging) before the six letters of the mnemonic “Yarmaluun”, that is Ya, Ra, Mim, Lam, Waw and Nun: with Ya, Nun, Mim and Waw the nun merges with Ghunnah, with Lam and Ra without Ghunnah — “min rabbihim” becomes “mir-rabbihim”, “min waliyyin” becomes “miw-waliyyin”. Iqlab (conversion) before the Ba: the nun becomes a mim with Ghunnah, “min ba'di” becomes “mim ba'di”. Ikhfa (concealing) before all the remaining fifteen letters: the nun is neither clear nor merged, but hinted at nasally, as in “min-kum” or “anzalnaa”. The Idgham applies only across a word boundary; within one word it is pronounced clearly.

For a vowelless mim there are three rules, all with the addition “shafawi” (of the lips). Idgham Shafawi: if a further mim follows, both merge into one doubled mim with Ghunnah, as in “lahum maa yashaa'uun”. Ikhfa Shafawi: if a Ba follows, the lips are only lightly closed, the mim is hinted at nasally and held with Ghunnah, for instance in “tarmiihim bi-hijaara”. Izhar Shafawi: before all the remaining letters the mim is pronounced clearly and without lengthening, as in “alaihim ghairi”. Particular care should be taken before Waw and Fa — because they too are formed at the lips, the mim easily blurs there, although it has to stay distinct.

Qalqalah means “shaking” and describes a short, springing echo that five letters receive when they are vowelless: Qaf, Ta, Ba, Jim and Dal — gathered in the mnemonic “Qutb Jad”. The letter is not given a vowel in the process, but only lightly released, so that you hear it without saying “qa”, “qi” or “qu”. A distinction is made between the small Qalqalah, when the letter carries a sukun in the middle of a word, like the Dal in “yadkhuluun”, and the great Qalqalah at the end of a word when stopping, for instance the Qaf in “al-falaq” — there it sounds more distinct, especially when a shadda stands as well. How strong the echo should turn out is described slightly differently in the textbooks; it should not be exaggerated.

The Ghunnah is a humming tone that arises in the nasal cavity and always belongs to nun and mim. It is clearest when one of the two carries a shadda: in “inna” or “thumma” the nasal sound is held for about two counts, as long as a natural long vowel. Ghunnah also accompanies several rules of the vowelless nun and mim: the Idgham with Ghunnah, the Iqlab, the Ikhfa and the Idgham Shafawi. Whether it really sounds is easily checked by holding the nose closed while speaking — then the tone must break off. The exact length is given uniformly in the textbooks as two counts; its strength can vary somewhat according to the rule and the teaching tradition.

Waqf is the stopping while reciting. Because you should not pause just anywhere in the middle of a sentence, most mushaf editions carry small letter signs above the line: mim means that you should stop, because reading on would change the sense; ta stands for a complete pause, jim for a permitted one; sad and za advise reading on rather than stopping; “la” means: do not stop here. Three dots that appear twice mark the mu'anaqa: you stop at one of the two places, never at both. When stopping, the last letter is pronounced without a vowel, a tanwin on fathah becomes a long “aa”, and a Ta Marbutah sounds like an “h”. These signs go back to later scholars such as as-Sajawandi and differ between printed editions — they are a reading aid, not part of the revealed text. If you have to take a breath unplanned, it is best to start again at the beginning of the word before it.

eintraege.titel: Common reading mistakes and how to avoid them
eintraege.text: The most common mistakes when reading the Quran concern similar-sounding letters that have no equivalent in English: ha, ha and kha; sin and sad; ta and ta; dal and dad; kaf and qaf. Mixing them up can change the meaning — “qalb” means heart, “kalb” by contrast means dog. Just as often the lengths are not held, or conversely short vowels are stretched, shaddas are swallowed and the Ghunnah is forgotten. Another classic is reading too fast: whoever rushes loses word endings and pauses at the same time. Three remedies help almost always — read slowly and aloud, record yourself and compare with a good recitation, and recite regularly to a teacher, because you rarely hear your own mistake. Mistakes while practising are no reason to stop: the way to correct reading leads exactly through them.

The Islamic calendar is a pure lunar calendar: twelve months, each beginning with the new moon, and a year has around 354 days. Because of this all Islamic dates move forward through the solar year by about eleven days each year — Ramadan can therefore fall in winter once and, years later, in high summer. The twelve months are called Muharram, Safar, Rabi' al-awwal, Rabi' ath-thani, Jumada l-ula, Jumada l-akhira, Rajab, Sha'ban, Ramadan, Shawwal, Dhul-Qa'dah and Dhul-Hijjah; four of them count as protected months. The counting runs from the Hijrah, the emigration of the Prophet ﷺ from Mecca to Medina — hence the designation “AH”. Because the beginning of a month can differ by one day depending on the country and the method (sighting or calculation), Muslims follow their local community.

Muharram is the first month of the Islamic year and one of the four protected months, in which wrongdoing weighs especially heavily. The tenth day is called Ashura; it is transmitted that the Prophet ﷺ fasted on this day and recommended the fast, because on it Allah rescued Musa and his people. Many Muslims therefore fast the ninth and tenth, or the tenth and eleventh of Muharram — voluntarily, not as an obligation. Ashura is moreover the day on which, in the year 61 AH, the Prophet's grandson al-Husayn was killed at Karbala; Shia Muslims observe it as a day of mourning, Sunni Muslims above all as a day of fasting. Rituals that go beyond the fasting are assessed differently — on this the local imam is the best person to advise.

Rabi' al-awwal is the third month of the Islamic year and closely bound up with the life of the Prophet ﷺ: in it he came into the world, in it he reached Quba on the edge of Yathrib after the Hijrah, and on Monday, the 12th of Rabi' al-awwal in the eleventh year AH, he passed away at the age of 63 in the room of his wife Aisha. In many countries the Mawlid is observed in this month — with recitation, talks on the Seerah and the feeding of people. Whether such celebrations are desirable is judged differently by scholars: some see in them a good opportunity to strengthen love for the Prophet ﷺ, others reject them as a later innovation. Undisputed is that love for the Prophet ﷺ shows itself above all in following his example in everyday life.

Rajab is the seventh month and belongs to the four protected months, in which fighting was traditionally forbidden and good as well as bad deeds carry particular weight. Sha'ban is the eighth month and thus the month directly before Ramadan; it is transmitted that the Prophet ﷺ fasted voluntarily a great deal in Sha'ban. Many Muslims therefore use these two months as a run-up: firming up the prayer times again, clearing debts and disputes, practising the fast and taking up the reading of the Quran. Around both months many special nights and rites have grown up regionally, which scholars assess very differently — here it is worth asking the local imam instead of relying on what is passed around.

Ramadan is the ninth month of the Islamic year and the month in which the Quran was sent down. For adult, healthy Muslims, fasting in it from dawn until sunset is an obligation and one of the five pillars of Islam; whoever is ill or travelling makes the days up later, and whoever permanently cannot fast feeds needy people instead. The month lives not only on doing without food and drink, but on prayer, reading of the Quran, generosity and patience in dealing with one another. In the last ten nights lies the Night of Decree (Laylat al-Qadr), which the Quran describes as better than a thousand months. Because the Islamic year is a lunar year, Ramadan shifts forward by about eleven days every year.
