eintraege.titel: Shawwal and the festival of breaking the fast
eintraege.text: Shawwal is the tenth month and begins with Eid al-Fitr, the festival of breaking the fast on the first day after Ramadan. To the festival belong the festival prayer in congregation, new or clean clothes, visits to family and neighbours — and, before the prayer, the Zakat al-Fitr, a small due for the needy so that they can celebrate too. The Quran names as the sense of concluding the fast that you complete the number of days and praise Allah for having guided you. It is also transmitted that six voluntary days of fasting in Shawwal, together with Ramadan, count like a whole year of fasting; they may be fasted consecutively or spread out. In Germany Eid al-Fitr is not a public holiday — many communities therefore hold the festival prayer early in the morning.

eintraege.titel: Dhul-Hijjah, Hajj and the festival of sacrifice
tags: when is the festival of sacrifice
eintraege.text: Dhul-Hijjah is the twelfth and last month of the Islamic year and the month of the pilgrimage. The Hajj to Mecca is an obligation once in a lifetime for every Muslim who is physically and financially in a position to do it. The first ten days of the month count as especially blessed days; their high point is the ninth day, the Day of Arafat, on which the pilgrims stand on the plain of Arafat and all other Muslims may fast voluntarily. On the tenth day follows Eid al-Adha, the festival of sacrifice, on which, in remembrance of Ibrahim, an animal is slaughtered and the meat is shared with family, neighbours and the needy. Whoever wants to sacrifice in Germany usually does so through an approved business or an aid organisation — the practical arrangement is best discussed with your own community.

tags: do i have to go to the mosque on friday
eintraege.text: Friday (Arabic al-Jumu'ah, “the day of gathering”) is the weekly high point for Muslims. Instead of the midday prayer, the Friday prayer is performed in the mosque: two units of prayer in congregation, preceded by an address (Khutbah). The Quran calls on the believers to let trade and business rest at the call to prayer on Friday and to hurry to the remembrance of Allah — and afterwards to go back to work. According to the majority of scholars taking part is an obligation for adult, locally resident men, while for women, travellers and the sick it is voluntary; in the details there are differences between the schools of law. In Germany Friday is a normal working day — many employees therefore arrange the prayer break with their employer well in advance. Recommended on this day are also the washing, clean clothes, reading Surah al-Kahf, and much prayer for the Prophet ﷺ.

Mecca lies in the west of the Arabian Peninsula and is the birthplace of the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ. At its centre stands the Kaaba, a cube-shaped building that the Quran describes as the first house of worship founded for humankind; Ibrahim and his son Isma'il raised its foundation walls and purified it for the worship of the one God. Before Islam around 360 idols stood around the Kaaba, until the Prophet ﷺ had them removed on his return to Mecca. The Kaaba is not worshipped: it is the Qibla, the shared direction of prayer that aligns Muslims worldwide — worshipped is Allah alone. Around it the pilgrims perform the Tawaf, the sevenfold circling.

Before the Hijrah, Medina was called Yathrib, and after the arrival of the Prophet ﷺ it was named Madinat an-Nabi, the city of the Prophet. On the way there he rested at Quba and founded the first mosque of Islam there. In Medina itself the Muslims built the Prophet's Mosque together out of mud bricks and palm trunks — the Prophet ﷺ carried stones himself like everyone else. It was far more than a place of prayer: school, meeting place, court and refuge for the poor, from whose shaded bench (Suffah) Companions without means learnt. In Medina the Prophet ﷺ also concluded the brotherhood between the emigrants from Mecca (Muhajirun) and the helpers of the city (Ansar), and agreed a common order of protection with the Jewish tribes living there. Today his grave is inside the Prophet's Mosque; for Muslims it counts as the second most important mosque after Mecca.

The al-Aqsa Mosque in Jerusalem is, after Mecca and Medina, the third especially honoured place of prayer for Muslims. The Quran opens Surah al-Isra with the night journey: Allah made His servant travel by night from the sacred place of prayer in Mecca to the farthest place of prayer, whose surroundings He has blessed; there the Prophet ﷺ led the earlier prophets in prayer. Jerusalem was moreover the first Qibla of the Muslims, until the direction of prayer was turned towards Mecca at Allah's instruction. In Islamic usage “al-Aqsa” mostly means the whole enclosed compound, to which the Dome of the Rock also belongs. The city is at the same time holy to Jews and Christians — the political situation there is disputed and is not part of basic religious knowledge.

eintraege.titel: The Hijrah — the emigration to Medina
eintraege.text: After years of persecution in Mecca the Muslims found allies in Yathrib: twelve men gave the first pledge of Aqaba, and a year later more than seventy men and women swore to protect the Prophet ﷺ as they would their own families. When the Quraysh decided to kill him, Ali lay down in his bed while the Prophet ﷺ left the house with Abu Bakr; for three days the two hid in the cave of Thawr, where Abu Bakr heard the words: “Do not be sad, Allah is with us.” After about two weeks on unfamiliar coastal paths they reached Quba on the edge of Yathrib. This emigration — in Arabic Hijrah, in the year 622 of the Christian era — later became the start of the Islamic era, because with it a persecuted group became a community. The Prophet ﷺ stressed in this connection that with every emigration what counts is the intention.
belege: an-Nawawī Nr. 1 — Sahih al-Bukhari 1, Sahih Muslim 1907

eintraege.text: After the death of the Prophet ﷺ in the year 632, four of his closest Companions led the community one after another; they are called the rightly guided caliphs. Abu Bakr as-Siddiq was chosen first, preserved the unity in the Riddah wars and had the Quran collected into a single volume for the first time. Umar ibn al-Khattab ruled for around ten years, lived more modestly than many of his subjects, created administration, a judiciary and a state welfare system, and was murdered in 644 during the Fajr prayer. Uthman ibn Affan had the uniform mushaf produced on the basis of the collected sheets and sent to the main cities — the text that Muslims recite to this day. Ali ibn Abi Talib was elected fourth caliph in 656, counted as an outstanding jurist and orator, and was murdered in Kufa in 661. The Prophet ﷺ had advised his community to hold fast to his Sunnah and to the Sunnah of the rightly guided caliphs.
belege: an-Nawawī Nr. 28 — Sunan Abu Dawud, Sunan at-Tirmidhi (sahih)

eintraege.text: Sahabah is the name for the Companions of the Prophet ﷺ: people who saw and accompanied him themselves as believers. They were not a uniform group but a cross-section of society — the merchant Khadijah, the wealthy Abu Bakr, the once enslaved Ethiopian Bilal, the learned Aisha, young and old, poor and rich. The Quran distinguishes between the Muhajirun, who emigrated from Mecca and left home and property behind, and the Ansar, the helpers from Medina, who shared their houses and harvests with them. Verses of the Quran were revealed about them, expressing Allah's pleasure with the foremost ones and with those who followed them sincerely. The Sahabah are important to Muslims because they are the transmitters of the Quran and of the Sunnah — what we know about the Prophet ﷺ came to us through them.

Sunnah literally means “way” or “custom” and denotes the transmitted way of life of the Prophet ﷺ: what he said, did and tacitly approved. The Quran calls him a beautiful example and instructs the believers to take what the Messenger gives them and to leave what he forbids. The Sunnah is thereby the second basic source of Islam alongside the Quran — it explains what the prayer, the fasting or the Zakat look like in practice, which the Quran itself does not describe in detail. Note: in everyday speech the word has a second, narrower meaning as well. When someone says “that is Sunnah”, they usually mean a recommended, voluntary act as opposed to the obligation (fard) — for example the voluntary units of prayer before and after the obligatory prayers. Which meaning is intended follows from the context.
belege: an-Nawawī Nr. 28 — Sunan Abu Dawud, Sunan at-Tirmidhi (sahih)

eintraege.text: A Hadith is a transmitted report about a statement, an action or an approval of the Prophet ﷺ. Every Hadith consists of two parts: the chain of transmitters (isnad) — who heard it from whom, back to a Companion — and the actual text (matn). Over centuries scholars examined the dates, the reputation and the accuracy of every single transmitter; out of this a science of Hadith criticism of its own arose. Roughly three levels are distinguished: sahih (sound, an unbroken chain of reliable transmitters), hasan (good, somewhat weaker but usable) and da'if (weak, for instance because of a gap in the chain or an unreliable transmitter). Well-known collections are Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim; the forty Hadith of an-Nawawi that are in this app come from them as well. Classifying individual reports is expert knowledge — not every statement circulating on the internet as a Hadith is genuine.

A madhhab is a school of law: a method, grown over centuries, of deriving concrete answers for everyday life from the Quran and the Sunnah. In Sunni Islam four are widespread — the Hanafi, the Maliki, the Shafi'i and the Hanbali; Shia Muslims follow, among others, the Ja'fari school. They do not differ in belief in Allah, in the Prophet ﷺ or in the Quran, but in questions of detail in practice: how the hands are held during the prayer, what makes the ablution invalid, how periods of time are calculated. This variety counts traditionally as a relief, not as a split — the Quran calls on you to ask the people of knowledge when you do not know something. As a beginner you do not have to commit yourself at once: mostly it is simplest to follow the practice of the local mosque and to ask about differences instead of switching between opinions.

eintraege.titel: What a fatwa is — and why the Salati AI does not give one
tags: am i allowed to do this
eintraege.text: A fatwa is the legal opinion of a qualified scholar (mufti) on a concrete question. It is not a judgement that forces anyone, but a reasoned answer to precisely that case — and it depends strongly on the circumstances: place, time, health, financial situation, applicable law. That is why the same question can have two different correct answers for two people, and why fatwas from the internet can rarely simply be transferred. The Quran expressly warns against saying about Allah what you do not know, and against following what you have no knowledge of. For this reason the Salati AI gives no fatwa: it can explain basic knowledge, show references and place terms in context — but it does not know your life situation, cannot ask you anything back and carries no responsibility. For personal questions the local imam or a recognised scholar is the right address.

tags: what am i allowed to eat
eintraege.text: The basic principle with food is permission: the Quran calls on people to eat of what is permitted and good on the earth. Expressly forbidden is only a small number of things — carrion, blood, pork, what was slaughtered in the name of someone other than Allah, and intoxicants. The Prophet ﷺ also taught that between the clearly permitted and the clearly forbidden lie doubtful things, and that whoever guards against them keeps his religion and his honour pure. In practice in Germany that means: read the ingredient lists (gelatine, lard, alcohol-based flavourings), ask when in doubt, and use certificates where they exist. How strictly individual additives, enzymes or traces of alcohol in flavourings are to be judged is assessed differently by scholars — with recurring doubtful cases a conversation with the local imam helps more than a quick answer from the internet.
belege: an-Nawawī Nr. 6 — Sahih al-Bukhari 52, Sahih Muslim 1599

tags: am i allowed to drink alcohol
eintraege.text: Intoxicating drinks are forbidden in Islam. The Quran names them together with gambling as an abomination from the work of Satan, which sows enmity and hatred and keeps people from the remembrance of Allah and from the prayer; elsewhere it says that their sin is greater than their benefit. The prohibition did not come all at once, but in stages — first the prohibition of coming to the prayer drunk, then the complete prohibition. It applies not only to the drinking itself, but also to production, trade and serving. How small quantities of alcohol in food, in medicines, in mouthwash or in alcohol-free beer with residual alcohol are to be handled is assessed differently by the schools of law; that is a question for the local imam. Whoever struggles with alcohol can also find professional addiction counselling in Germany — seeking help is no contradiction to faith.

tags: am i allowed to eat pork
eintraege.text: Pork belongs to the few things that the Quran expressly and repeatedly names as forbidden — alongside carrion, blood, and that over which a name other than Allah's was invoked. A reason is not given at length; Muslims follow the prohibition as an instruction from Allah, not because of a medical justification. In practice this also concerns products made from the pig, for instance lard and gelatine in sweets, yoghurt or capsules — here a look at the ingredient list is worthwhile. At the same time the Quran makes an express exception: whoever is in a genuine emergency, without craving it and without overstepping the limit, bears no sin. If you have eaten something by mistake, that is no reason to panic: you consciously renounce it, ask Allah for forgiveness and pay attention to it in future.

eintraege.titel: Islamic slaughter and meat in the West
tags: food of the people of the book
eintraege.text: In Islamic slaughter the animal is killed with a sharp knife by a quick cut to the throat, and the name of Allah is spoken while doing so. The Prophet ﷺ taught that excellence is to be kept in slaughtering too: to sharpen the blade and to spare the animal. Forbidden is the meat of animals that died of themselves, were strangled or beaten to death, or over which a name other than Allah's was invoked. In Europe the matter is made more complicated by the fact that animal-welfare law in many countries requires stunning before the cut, that much poultry is slaughtered by machine, and that “halal” is not a uniformly protected term. Exactly here the opinions of scholars diverge: some accept a reversible stunning and additionally invoke the verse that permits the food of the People of the Book, others reject stunning and machine slaughter. Whoever wants to be sure buys from a butcher whose procedure he knows, or follows the guidance of his local imam; when in doubt the advice applies to leave what raises doubt.
belege: an-Nawawī Nr. 11 — Jami' at-Tirmidhi 2518, Sunan an-Nasa'i 5711

eintraege.text: Riba denotes interest, or the unlawful increase that arises without a counter-performance and without shared risk. The Quran forbids it clearly and states that Allah has permitted trade and forbidden interest; whoever still has open interest transactions should leave them, but keeps the capital he put in — so that neither wrong is done nor suffered. The thought behind it is that profit should arise from real performance and shared risk, not from the hardship of others. In everyday life in Germany this raises many practical questions: current account, building savings contract, purchase by instalments, mortgage financing, default interest, occupational pension schemes. On these there are various positions among scholars — from strict avoidance, through the use of Islam-compliant financing models, to exceptions in emergencies. This is a typical question for personal advice from a scholar or the local imam, not for a blanket answer.

tags: do i have to wear a headscarf
eintraege.text: The Quran addresses the instruction to restraint first to the men: they are to lower their gaze and guard their chastity. Immediately afterwards the same applies to the women, supplemented by the instruction to draw their headscarves over the opening of their garment at the breast and not to display their adornment openly. Undisputed with this is a shared core: clothing should cover, should not be see-through or provocative, and decency concerns both sexes. About the details there are differences between the schools of law — for instance which parts of the body may stay visible for women outside the family, and how exactly the area between navel and knee is to be understood for men; the face veil counts for the majority as voluntary, not as an obligation. At the same time the Quran recalls that the best clothing is that of God-consciousness. For women who have converted and for newcomers it holds: this grows with time, happens without compulsion, and is no yardstick for judging others.

Marriage counts in Islam as one of the most beautiful institutions and is described as a sign of Allah: He created spouses so that you may find rest with them, and placed affection and mercy between them. The Quran calls the marriage bond a firm covenant and describes the spouses as a garment for one another — as protection, closeness and dignity. To the conclusion of a marriage belong, by general agreement, the free consent of both, offer and acceptance, witnesses, as well as a bridal gift (Mahr) for the wife, which belongs to her alone. Forced marriage is not permissible and is moreover a criminal offence in Germany. In the details the schools of law differ — for instance in the role of the bride's guardian (wali), in the number of witnesses and in questions of form. Important for Germany: a religious wedding alone establishes no claims in civil law; the civil marriage at the registry office protects both sides. For carrying it out concretely, the local mosque is the right place to turn to.

The Quran sums the relationship of the spouses up in one principle: deal with one another in a lawful, good way — and women have the same due towards men as men have towards them. From this scholars derive shared basic rights: respect, faithfulness, conversation, physical and emotional attention, keeping the other's secrets. Classically an additional division of roles is described, in which the husband provides the maintenance, while the wife's property belongs to her alone; how that looks in practice today in a marriage with two working partners is answered differently by scholars and, within the bounds of what is permitted, is a matter of agreement. Undisputed, by contrast, is this: the Prophet ﷺ taught the principle that there is no harm and no inflicting of harm. Domestic violence cannot be justified with any of this — it is wrongdoing and a criminal offence in Germany. Whoever is affected may and should get help: at the helpline for violence against women, at counselling centres and, if necessary, from the police.

tags: how do i raise my child islamically
eintraege.text: The Quran shows upbringing through the example of Luqman, who first lays the core of faith on his son's heart — to associate nothing with Allah — and then guides him to perform the prayer, to enjoin what is right, to forbid what is wrong and to bear patiently what strikes him. Remarkable is the tone: Luqman addresses his son again and again with “my dear son”, that is, with affection, not with harshness. Elsewhere the believers are called upon to guard themselves and their families, and the Prophet ﷺ is instructed to urge his family to prayer and to be steadfast in it himself — one's own practice therefore comes before the admonition. In practice that means: take them along early and lovingly instead of forcing them, explain in a way suited to their age, pray and read together, forgive mistakes and build trust. Corporal punishment is forbidden by law in Germany and is not compatible with the merciful way the Prophet ﷺ dealt with children.

eintraege.titel: Keeping up the ties of kinship
eintraege.text: Keeping up the ties of kinship, in Arabic Silat ar-Rahim, carries great weight in Islam. The Quran names the ties of kinship directly alongside God-consciousness, praises those who join what Allah has commanded to be joined, and censures the tearing apart of the ties as corruption. Parents are especially singled out: you are to be kind to them, not to snap at them in old age, to speak respectfully with them and to pray for them — and the Quran recalls in particular the effort of the mother, who carried in weakness upon weakness. This applies expressly even when the parents are not Muslim; for many converts that is an important clarification. Keeping up the ties does not mean accepting every wrong: where a relationship is harmful, you may keep your distance and still stay friendly, pray for the person and leave the door open. In practice small things are often enough — a phone call, a visit, a greeting at the festival.

The Quran states soberly that every soul will taste death and that this worldly life is only a passing enjoyment. When Muslims learn of a person's death, they therefore speak the words that the Quran ascribes to those who endure: “We belong to Allah, and to Him we return.” Mourning is permitted and human — the Prophet ﷺ too wept for his son; forbidden by the reports is only the excessive wailing that quarrels with Allah's decree. In practice standing by someone means: visiting the family, bringing food, asking forgiveness for the person who has died, answering the children in a way suited to their age. By the reports a person's deeds end with death, except an ongoing charity, useful knowledge and a righteous child who prays for them — which is why the supplication for the deceased is so important. The Prophet ﷺ advised living in this world like a stranger or a wayfarer.

tags: how does an islamic funeral work
eintraege.text: When a Muslim dies, it belongs to the duties of the community to wash him (ghusl), to wrap him in plain white cloths (kafan), to perform the funeral prayer and to bury him. These tasks count as fard kifayah: if a part of the community carries them out, the duty is fulfilled for everyone. The funeral prayer itself is short and is performed standing, without bowing and without prostration — four takbir, and between them the opening Surah, the prayer for the Prophet ﷺ and a supplication for the person who has died; afterwards the Salam follows. The burial should take place without unnecessary delay, usually without a coffin, on the right side with the face towards the Qibla, with a plain grave. In Germany the burial laws of the federal states regulate deadlines, the requirement of a coffin and grave fields differently; many cities now have Muslim grave fields. Practical questions — burial without a coffin, transfer, deadlines — are best clarified early with the community and an experienced undertaker. The Quran recalls the simple thought behind it: from the earth we were created, into it we return, and out of it we will be brought forth another time.

tags: how is inheritance divided in islam
eintraege.text: The Quran regulates the order of inheritance in unusual detail and lays down that both men and women are entitled to a fixed share of the estate of parents and closest relatives — at a time when women in many places had no right of inheritance at all. Concrete quotas are named for children, parents, spouses and siblings, in each case after the deduction of debts and of a bequest. That a son in certain constellations receives twice as much as a daughter stands in connection with the maintenance duties that are classically assigned to the man, while the wife's property belongs to her alone; other constellations lead to other ratios. The concrete calculation is a field of its own (Ilm al-Fara'id) and cannot be done from memory. For Muslims in Germany there is the additional point that German inheritance law with its compulsory-share claims applies here in principle; whoever wants to order their estate islamically needs a will for it and should take advice both from a scholar or the local imam and from a lawyer.

eintraege.titel: How to behave in the mosque
tags: may a non-muslim enter a mosque
eintraege.text: A mosque is first of all a place of prayer: the Quran says that the places of worship belong to Allah and that no one is to be called upon besides Him. Customary are a few simple things: take your shoes off at the entrance, come clean and neatly dressed, be quiet, do not walk in front of people praying, put the phone on silent, and on entering with the right foot perform two short units of prayer to greet the mosque, if there is time for it just then. In most mosques men and women pray in separate areas. The Quran recalls putting on your adornment — that is, well-kept clothing — at every place of worship, and at the same time not being excessive. Guests and non-Muslims are as a rule welcome, especially on the open mosque day; a short note at the entrance or a question to someone on site settles questions of dress and the right time to come. Whoever comes for the first time may happily say that they are new — usually someone is glad to help.

Besides the obligatory due Zakat, Islam knows the voluntary donation (Sadaqah), which can be given at any time and in any amount. The Quran compares it with a grain of seed that makes seven ears grow, each with a hundred grains, and states that you reach true goodness only when you give of what is dear to you. For Zakat the Quran names eight groups of recipients, among them the poor, the needy, the indebted and travellers in need. Sadaqah is not limited to money: the Prophet ﷺ taught that a good word, a just settlement between people, help with carrying, every step towards the prayer and even the removal of an obstacle from the path are Sadaqah — so even whoever has little can give. A waqf is a lasting endowment: a piece of land, a well, a mosque or a school is irrevocably dedicated to a good purpose, so that the benefit flows on continuously. A well-known example is the well of Rumah, which Uthman ibn Affan bought and released to the community forever.
belege: an-Nawawī Nr. 26 — Sahih al-Bukhari, Sahih Muslim

eintraege.text: Mistakes are part of being human — what is decisive is what comes after them. The Quran addresses one of the most comforting verses of all to everyone who has been excessive against themselves: they should not lose hope in Allah's mercy, for Allah forgives all sins. Sincere repentance (tawbah) consists classically of four steps: stop the deed, regret it, resolve firmly not to return to it — and, if a person has been harmed, make the wrong good again or ask for pardon. No intermediary and no confession before others is needed for it; not spreading out your own mistakes in public even counts as better. The Prophet ﷺ transmitted from Allah that He forgives as long as a person calls upon Him and hopes in Him — even if the sins were almost as great as the earth. And his practical advice was: fear Allah wherever you are; let a good deed follow a bad one, it wipes it out; and meet people with good character.
belege: an-Nawawī Nr. 42 — Sunan at-Tirmidhi (hasan, Hadith Qudsi)
